How Global Calibration Strengthens Multiaccuracy

Sílvia Casacuberta Affiliation: University of Oxford    Parikshit Gopalan Affiliation: Apple    Varun Kanade Affiliation: University of Oxford    Omer Reingold Affiliation: Stanford University
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Multiaccuracy and multicalibration are multigroup fairness notions for prediction that have found numerous applications in learning and computational complexity [24]. They can be achieved from a single learning primitive: weak agnostic learning. A line of work starting from [18] has shown that multicalibration implies a very strong form of learning. Here we investigate the power of multiaccuracy as a learning primitive, both with and without the additional assumption of calibration. We find that multiaccuracy in itself is rather weak, but that the addition of global calibration (this notion is called calibrated multiaccuracy) boosts its power substantially, enough to recover implications that were previously known only assuming the stronger notion of multicalibration.

We give evidence that multiaccuracy might not be as powerful as standard weak agnostic learning, by showing that there is no way to post-process a multiaccurate predictor to get a weak learner, even assuming the best hypothesis has correlation 1/21/2. Rather, we show that it yields a restricted form of weak agnostic learning, which requires some concept in the class to have correlation greater than 1/21/2 with the labels. However, by also requiring the predictor to be calibrated, we recover not just weak, but strong agnostic learning.

A similar picture emerges when we consider the derivation of hardcore measures from predictors satisfying multigroup fairness notions [46, 8]. On the one hand, while multiaccuracy only yields hardcore measures of density half the optimal, we show that (a weighted version of) calibrated multiaccuracy achieves optimal density.

Our results yield new insights into the complementary roles played by multiaccuracy and calibration in each setting. They shed light on why multiaccuracy and global calibration, although not particularly powerful by themselves, together yield considerably stronger notions.

1 Introduction

A major line of research within the algorithmic fairness community focuses on the notion of multicalibration, first introduced by Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold, and Rothblum [24]. This concept centers on risk predictors that estimate individual probabilities for outcomes such as: what is the likelihood that an individual will repay a loan, successfully complete their studies, or be hired after an interview? These predictive tasks often inform high-stakes decisions—granting loans, admitting applicants to universities, or extending job interview invitations—and thus raise critical fairness concerns. Multicalibration requires that predictions be calibrated across a rich and potentially intersecting collection of subpopulations. A predictor is said to be calibrated on a subpopulation if, for individuals to whom it assigns a probability vv of a given outcome, approximately a vv fraction of them actually experience that outcome. In other words, the predictions should “mean what they say” not just globally, but also within each relevant subpopulation.

While multicalibration gained widespread acceptance as an appealing fairness criterion, this paper focuses on its interaction with concepts from other domains, specifically complexity theory and computational learning theory. Multicalibration draws from both fields. It is naturally viewed as a complexity-theoretic perspective on fairness, as it asks for predictors to be able to pass a rich class of computationally-defined tests. This connection has been sharpened through the lens of outcome indistinguishability [10]. From the standpoint of learning theory, multicalibration is only meaningful as a fairness notion if it is computationally attainable. The algorithms used to learn multicalibrated predictors rely on foundational concepts from learning theory, such as weak agnostic learning and agnostic boosting [3, 39, 31, 30, 13].

A large body of work has shown deep connections in the other direction; namely, exploring the impact of multicalibration and its relaxations to complexity theory and learning. Most relevant to this paper, multicalibration implies a strong form of loss minimization called omniprediction [18, 17, 20, 41] and constructions of hardcore distributions in computational complexity [8]. Some of the other implications are the notion of domain adaptation [33], and additional complexity-theoretic applications [11, 26, 8, 40]. In the application of multicalibration to computational complexity and learning theory, it is natural to ask whether multicalibration is truly necessary and what the minimal underlying assumptions are. Beyond potential efficiency improvements, our goal is to offer new insights into the fundamental concepts of agnostic learning and hardcore distributions.

Calibrated Multiaccuracy.

Multiaccuracy [46, 24, 34] is a weaker notion of multigroup fairness. Like multicalibration, it is parameterized by a family of subpopulations 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For the purposes of this discussion, we can assume that each c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} is a Boolean function, that is, the characteristic function of a set.11 1 The formal definition allows for real-valued functions which can be interpreted as encoding fuzzy set membership. In multiaccuracy, we require that for each c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}, the expected prediction over individuals in the set defined by cc is approximately equal to the fraction of those individuals who experience a positive outcome. Hence, such predictors are accurate on average for each such cc. In this work, we explore the power of multiaccuracy as a primitive in computational learning and in the context of hardcore distributions. In both settings, a common theme arises: multiaccuracy alone is insufficient to achieve our desired guarantees.

However, when we supplement multiaccuracy (or a weighted variant thereof) with global calibration—that is, calibration over the entire population rather than all subgroups in 𝒞\mathcal{C}—we recover many of the appealing consequences of multicalibration. This strengthened notion, referred to as calibrated multiaccuracy, has already demonstrated its utility in prior work on omnipredictors via outcome indistinguishability [17]. In [17], it is also argued that calibrated multiaccuracy can be more efficient to achieve than full multicalibration, and costs about the same as multiaccuracy. For this reason, our results give efficiency improvements compared with basing the applications we consider on multicalibration instead. Furthermore, by clarifying the distinct but complementary contributions of multiaccuracy and global calibration in each application, this work offers new insights on these fundamental notions.

Computational learning.

Multicalibrated predictors with respect to a family 𝒞\mathcal{C} can be learned from a sample of individuals and outcome pairs via a learning primitive known as weak agnostic learning for 𝒞\mathcal{C} [24]. Weak agnostic learning allows learning a hypothesis that is somewhat correlated with the labels as long as some hypothesis in 𝒞\mathcal{C} is sufficiently correlated [3, 31, 30, 13]. Quantitatively, assuming the existence of a hypothesis in 𝒞\mathcal{C} that achieves correlation α>0\alpha>0, an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) weak learner returns a hypothesis with correlation at least β\beta. Typically, one hopes to get β=poly⁡(α)\beta=\poly(\alpha) even when α\alpha approaches 00. This should be contrasted with (strong) agnostic learning, where a hypothesis can be found that is almost as correlated with the data as the best hypothesis in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} is; in other words β≥α−ε\beta\geq\alpha-\varepsilon.

A line of work [18, 17, 20, 41] shows that multicalibration implies a strong form of learning called omniprediction that allows for the simultaneous minimization of all convex, Lipschitz loss functions. All one needs to do is to post-process the predictions with a best-response function. This a very broad guarantee. Specializing to the case of correlation loss tells us that multicalibration implies a strong agnostic learning algorithm, where the post-processing function here corresponds to sign⁡(p−1/2)\mathrm{sign}(p-1/2). Thus, agnostic learning is both necessary and sufficient for multicalibration.

Can the same be said about multiaccuracy? Obviously, weak agnostic learning is sufficient for multiaccuracy (which is a weaker notion than multicalibration), and the original multiaccuracy algorithm from [24] builds a multiaccurate predictor by repeatedly calling a weak agnostic learner. But, is it necessary? While it seems intuitive that the answer should be yes, this paper paints a much more subtle picture:

  • •

    Perhaps surprisingly, we give evidence that multiaccuracy in itself need not imply weak agnostic learning in the standard sense. We prove the existence of a class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, a distribution on labels, and a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate predictor pp such that even though there is hypothesis in 𝒞\mathcal{C} that gives correlation 1/21/2, no post-processing of the predictor has any non-zero correlation with the labels. Furthermore, we show that this is the case for all classes 𝒞\mathcal{C} for which there exist of pseudorandom functions that fool 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

  • •

    We complement this lower bound by showing that multiaccuracy does imply weak learning once the correlation α\alpha exceeds 1/21/2: If there is a hypothesis in 𝒞\mathcal{C} with correlation α\alpha, then sign⁡(p−1/2)\mathrm{sign}(p-1/2) where pp is (𝒞,0)(\mathcal{C},0)-multiaccurate achieves correlation β=2​α−1\beta=2\alpha-1, a guarantee that is only non-trivial when α>1/2\alpha>1/2. We call this restricted weak agnostic learning, to contrast it with the standard notion of weak agnostic learning where α\alpha approaches 00.

  • •

    In contrast, we show that if the predictor pp is both 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate and calibrated, then sign⁡(p−1/2)\mathrm{sign}(p-1/2) is a strong agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C}, whose correlation is at least that of the best hypothesis in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Thus, the addition of calibration considerably increases the power of the predictor.

  • •

    Given the agnostic boosting results of [30, 13] that show that (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learning can be boosted to (γ,γ−α)(\gamma,\gamma-\alpha)-weak learning for any γ>α\gamma>\alpha, one might wonder, if boosting in the opposite direction is possible, i.e., given an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak learner, can we design an (α′,β′)(\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime})-weak learner for α′<α\alpha^{\prime}<\alpha? We answer this question in the negative under standard cryptographic assumptions.

  • •

    Lastly, the result of [24] shows that (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learning achieves a multiaccuracy parameter of α\alpha; we show that in general, given such a weak learner, it is not possible to achieve multiaccuracy parameter better than α/2\alpha/2.

Hardcore set constructions.

Impagliazzo’s hardcore lemma is a fundamental result in computational complexity that relates a function gg being (mildly) δ\delta-hard to predict under a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} for distinguishers in a class 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} to the existence of a hardcore measure μ\mu of density Ω⁡(δ)\Omega(\delta) in 𝒟\mathcal{D}, such that gg is 1/2−ε1/2-\varepsilon-hard to predict (i.e., one cannot improve over random guessing) when sampling from the measure to distinguishers from a family 𝒞⊂𝒞q\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{C}_{q}. The parameter qq measures the number of 𝒞\mathcal{C}-gates required for functions in 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q}. The larger qq is, the stronger the hardness assumption we make to show the existence of a hardcore distribution for 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

The work of Trevisan, Tulsiani, and Vadhan [46], which preceded the literature on multigroup fairness, gave an elegant connection to multiaccuracy, showing how to get a simple and explicit hardcore measure from a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate predictor.22 2 As pointed out in [11, 8], the notion of (𝒞,ϵ)(\mathcal{C},\epsilon)-indistinguishability in complexity theory, as used in [46], is exactly equivalent to the notion of (𝒞,ϵ)(\mathcal{C},\epsilon)-multiaccuracy as defined in the multigroup fairness literature. Their construction, however, achieves a hardcore measure of density δ\delta, while the optimal density is 2​δ2\delta [25]. Recently, Casacuberta, Dwork, and Vadhan [8] showed that multicalibration implies a stronger form of the hardcore lemma, which they call ICHL+⁣+++. From this they derive the original hardcore lemma by Impagliazzo, this time with a hardcore measure of optimal density 2​δ2\delta. However, while [46] achieve q=O⁡(1/ε2​δ2)q=O(1/\varepsilon^{2}\delta^{2}), [8] get q=O⁡(1/(ε12​δ6))q=O(1/(\varepsilon^{12}\delta^{6})).33 3 The stronger bound of O⁡(1/(ε2​δ2))O(1/(\varepsilon^{2}\delta^{2})) stated in [8] appears not to be correct. We refer the reader to a detailed discussion at the end of Section 5.3. This increased complexity comes in part because achieving multicalibration requires more calls to a (strong) agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C}, in contrast to multiaccuracy.

We show how to construct hardcore distributions with optimal density 2​δ2\delta as in [8] but with the lower complexity bound of q=O⁡(1/(ε2​δ2))q=O(1/(\varepsilon^{2}\delta^{2})) for 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} as in [46]. Indeed, we give a simple and explicit form for such a measure, starting from a predictor satisfying calibration and a weighted variant of multiaccuracy that we call weighted multiaccuracy. Recall that in multiaccuracy we ask that the expected prediction on every set is accurate. In weighted multiaccuracy we instead consider a weighted average (modified by a fixed function of the predictions where we weigh individuals with prediction value closer to half more). Both calibration and weighted multiaccuracy are implied by multicalibration, so this gives an alternate proof of the optimal density result of [8]. But crucially, the cost of obtaining both these conditions together (by many measures, including oracle calls to the weak learner) is not much more than that of multiaccuracy, which yields a considerably better bound on the parameter qq.

The three tiers of multigroup fairness.

As shown in Figure 1, our work together with the results of [46, 8, 20] paints a clear picture of the relative power of various multigroup fairness notions in the context of learning and hardcore measure constructions. Arrows represent implications that either follow by definition or through post-processing the underlying object. When more powerful oracle reductions are allowed, all these notions are achievable using (weak) agnostic learning.

The tiers are anchored by multiaccuracy, calibrated multiaccuracy and multicalibration respectively. For simplicity, we ignore the differences between swap multicalibration and standard multicalibration, and weighted multiaccuracy and standard multiaccuracy, since the computational costs of these notions are roughly the same.

  • •

    Multicalibration: the top tier. Multicalibration implies the strongest known form of the Impagliazzo hardcore lemma, namely the IHCL+⁣+++ [8]. On the learning front, it implies several strong forms of learning: swap agnostic learning and swap omniprediction (we refer the readers to [18, 20] for the definitions of these notions). It however comes at the cost of higher complexity of learning, more complex predictors (in terms of circuit size) and higher sample complexity.

  • •

    Calibrated Multiaccuracy: the Goldilocks zone. On the learning front, calibrated multiaccuracy implies strong agnostic learning and loss OI for generalized linear models (see [17] for definitions). On the hardcore lemma front, it gives hardcore sets of optimal density 2​δ2\delta, but with relatively low blowup in qq. The computational, and representational, costs are much lower than multicalibration, and comparable to multiaccuracy. But it is not as powerful as full-blown multicalibration, and does not imply IHCL+⁣+++ or swap agnostic learning (see [20] for the latter separation).

  • •

    Multiaccuracy: the lowest rung. Multiaccuracy implies hardcore sets of density δ\delta by [46]. On the learning front, it does not give weak agnostic learning for α≤1/2\alpha\leq 1/2, using post-processing. It does give restricted weak agnostic learning for α>1/2\alpha>1/2. The key argument in its favor is that it is cheap and easy to achieve, both in theory and practice: minimizing squared loss or running a GLM over a base class 𝒞\mathcal{C} is guaranteed to yield multiaccurate predictors [17].

Independent of our work, Pranay Tankala has observed that getting optimal density 2​δ2\delta in the IHCL was possible under weaker multigroup fairness conditions than multicalibration [45].

The case for calibrated multiaccuracy.

The power of multicalibration [24, 10, 18] illustrates the potency of combining calibration and multiaccuracy. But this great power comes at a high computational price. Our results show that in two important settings, agnostic learning and hardcore set constructions, global calibration together with multiaccuracy is a cheaper alternative to multicalibration, adding weight to a thesis that was first put forth by [17]. Our proofs highlight the complementary roles that multiaccuracy and calibration play, and give clear intuition for why their combination succeeds even when they each fail in isolation. In concurrent work, Hu and Vadhan use the notion of calibrated multiaccuracy to provide pseudoentropy characterizations for general entropy notions [27]. A deep insight in theoretical computer science has been that hardness and learning are two sides of the same coin [28, 35, 46, 13]; our work provides further evidence of this phenomenon.

We believe that these theoretical results also offer some insights to practice. As pointed out in the work of [17], some form of multiaccuracy is achieved by commonly used machine learning models that perform empirical risk minimization with a proper loss. Such a model will not likely be calibrated as is; see the discussion in [5]. But calibrated multiaccuracy is not much harder to achieve, and it can be easily implemented using standard libraries for calibration and regression, in contrast to full-blown multicalibration which is not easily implemented via standard libraries.44 4 While implementations do exist [43, 14, 23], experiments have found that its sample complexity is fairly large in contrast with multiaccuracy [21]. The argument for adding calibration is typically that calibration is a nice property to have, and it does not harm the loss (as long as it is proper). Our work gives a more compelling argument; namely, that global calibration significantly bolsters the power of a predictive model beyond multiaccuracy, without incurring much additional cost.

2 Overview of our Results

In this section, we describe our main results in more detail and explain the key ideas behind them. For this, we quickly recap some notation and definitions, leaving a more formal treatment to Section 3.

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote a distribution over pairs (𝐱,𝐲)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) where 𝐱∈𝒳\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X} denotes a point and 𝐲∈{0,1}\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\} its label. All expectations unless mentioned otherwise refer to this distribution. A predictor is a function p:𝒳→{0,1}p:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} while a hypothesis class 𝒞={c:𝒳→[−1,1]}\mathcal{C}=\{c:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1]\} is a collection of bounded functions, which we assume is closed under negation and contains the constant 𝟏\mathbf{1} function. The Bayes optimal predictor is p∗​(𝐱)=𝐄[𝐲|𝐱]p^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\E[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}]. We will think of functions from 𝒳→ℝ\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} as vectors with the inner product ⟨p,q⟩=𝐄[p⁡(𝐱)​q​(𝐱)]\langle p,q\rangle=\E[p(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x})].

Multigroup fairness notions.

The notion of (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccuracy as defined in [24] requires that

maxc∈𝒞|𝐄𝒟[c⁡(𝐱)​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))]|≤τ.\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\Bigl\lvert\E_{\mathcal{D}}[c(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))]\Bigr\rvert\leq\tau.

For intuition, let τ=0\tau=0. In this case multiaccuracy requires that for every c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}, we have

𝐄[c⁡(𝐱)​(p∗​(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱))]=0,\E[c(\mathbf{x})(p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x}))]=0,

or equivalently that every c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} is orthogonal to p−p∗p-p^{*}. Hence pp and p∗p^{*} both have the same projection onto the subspace spanned by 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Calibration is a classic notion from the forecasting literature [9]. Perfect calibration asks that 𝐄[𝐲|p⁡(𝐱)]=p⁡(𝐱)\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]=p(\mathbf{x}), in other words, conditioned on any prediction value vv, the expectation of the label is exactly vv. We say that the predictor is τ\tau-calibrated if

𝐄[|𝐄[𝐲|p(𝐱)]−p(𝐱))|]≤τ.\E[|\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]-p(\mathbf{x}))|]\leq\tau.

Calibrated multiaccuracy introduced in [17], asks for predictors that are both multiaccurate and calibrated, as the name suggests. It is a stronger requirement than just multiaccuracy, although of comparable sample and computational complexity [17, Section 7].

Multicalibration [24] is a further strengthening of calibrated multiaccuracy. We say that pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multicalibrated if

maxc∈𝒞⁡𝐄[|c⁡(𝐱)​(𝐄[𝐲|p⁡(𝐱)]−p⁡(𝐱))|]≤τ.\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\E[|c(\mathbf{x})(\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]-p(\mathbf{x}))|]\leq\tau.

If we take c=1c=\mathrm{1}, we recover calibration, and if we ignore the absolute values in the outer expectation, we recover multiaccuracy.

Agnostic learning.

We define weak and strong agnostic learning following [3, 32, 31, 30, 13]. The correlation between a function c:𝒳→[−1,1]c:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1] and the labels is defined as cor𝒟​(𝐲,c)=𝐄[c⁡(𝐱)​(2​𝐲−1)]∈[−1,1]\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c)=\E[c(\mathbf{x})(2\mathbf{y}-1)]\in[-1,1], where the map 𝐲↦2​𝐲−1\mathbf{y}\mapsto 2\mathbf{y}-1 maps labels in {0,1}\{0,1\} to {±1}\{\pm 1\}. A β\beta-weak learner is a function h:𝒳→[−1,1]h:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1] such that cor⁡(𝐲,h)≥β\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},h)\geq\beta. Taking h=0h=0 which gives 00 correlation as our baseline, we would like β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1] to be as large as possible. For a predictor p:𝒳→{0,1}p:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}, we will often use the transformation p↦2​p−1p\mapsto 2p-1. This maps the p=1/2p=1/2 predictor to h=0h=0, corresponding to the fact that guessing randomly at every point gives 00 correlation.

For α≥β∈[0,1]\alpha\geq\beta\in[0,1], an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} is an algorithm that has access to a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} (with a known marginal 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} over 𝒳\mathcal{X}). If 𝒟\mathcal{D} is such that if there exists a hypothesis cc such that cor⁡(𝐲,c)≥α\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c)\geq\alpha, the algorithm is guaranteed to return a β\beta-weak learner. It helps to think of β\beta as smaller than but polynomially related to α\alpha. In contrast, a strong agnostic learner must return a hypothesis that achieves correlation Opt⁡(𝒞)−ε\mathrm{Opt}(\mathcal{C})-\varepsilon where Opt⁡(𝒞)=maxc∈𝒞⁡cor⁡(𝐲,c)\mathrm{Opt}(\mathcal{C})=\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c) for every ε>0\varepsilon>0. The agnostic boosting results of [30, 13] imply that an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) weak learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} can be boosted to a hypothesis that gives correlation at least Opt⁡(𝒞)−α−ε\mathrm{Opt}(\mathcal{C})-\alpha-\varepsilon. Thus, given a weak learner that can handle arbitrarily small correlation α\alpha, we can achieve strong agnostic learning.55 5 The parameter β\beta only affects the number of iterations of boosting, hence it is less important than α\alpha.

Multigroup fairness and agnostic learning.

Results of [24, 17] show that all of multiaccuracy, calibrated multiaccuracy, and multicalibration with error τ\tau can be achieved using an (τ,β)(\tau,\beta) weak agnostic learner as an oracle. The algorithms will involve multiple calls to the weak agnostic learner. The number of calls grows as O⁡(1/β2)O(1/\beta^{2}) for multiaccuracy and calibrated multiaccuracy, and O⁡(1/τ2​β4)O(1/\tau^{2}\beta^{4}) for multicalibration. The added complexity in multicalibration comes from having to ensure multiaccuracy holds for prediction values that have fairly small probability, see the detailed discussion in [17, Section 7.3].

Our goal is to understand the relative strengths of the various multigroup fairness notions for agnostic learning. More precisely, given a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate predictor pp, when can we post-process its predictions (by some function k:[0,1]→[−1,1]k:[0,1]\to[-1,1]) to get a weak agnostic learner? Here is what was known before:

  • •

    When pp is multicalibrated, then sign⁡(p−1/2)\mathrm{sign}(p-1/2) is a strong agnostic learner. This is an implication of a general result proved in [18], that a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multicalibrated pp is an omnipredictor for all convex Lipschitz loss functions. This means that for every such loss ℓ\ell, there is a post-processing function kℓk_{\ell} so that kℓ​(p)k_{\ell}(p) suffers a loss comparable to the best hypothesis in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The implication for agnostic learning comes from considering the (negation of) correlation as a loss.

  • •

    When 𝒞={c:𝒳→{±1}}\mathcal{C}=\{c:\mathcal{X}\to\{\pm 1\}\} is a family of Boolean rather than bounded functions, then correlation coincides with the 00-11 loss. In this setting, the work of [17] shows that if pp satisfies calibrated multiaccuracy, then it is an omnipredictor, using the technique of loss outcome indistinguishability. This implies that the hypothesis sign⁡(p−1/2)\mathrm{sign}(p-1/2) is a strong agnostic learner.

We are unaware of work that considered multiaccuracy as a learning primitive. In light of the above results, it would be natural to guess that multiaccuracy ought to imply (at least) weak agnostic learning. This would tightly characterize weak agnostic learning as being necessary and sufficient for all the multigroup fairness notion above. Perhaps surprisingly, the answer is more nuanced.

2.1 Agnostic Learning and Multiaccuracy: With and Without Calibration

We start with the observation that weak learning is essentially equivalent to non-trivial square loss minimization, that beats random guessing. This observation is not entirely new, but will help elucidate several of our results.

Assume that hh is a β\beta-weak learner. Then, as observed by [24], taking a standard gradient step, the predictor p⁡(𝐱)=(1+β​h​(𝐱))/2p(\mathbf{x})=(1+\beta h(\mathbf{x}))/2 satisfies

𝐄[(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))2]≤𝐄[(𝐲−12)2]−3​β24.\displaystyle\E[(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]\leq\E\left[\left(\mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right]-\frac{3\beta^{2}}{4}.

In other words, weak agnostic learning enables non-trivial squared loss minimization, when compared to random guessing.

In the other direction, we show that any function h:𝒳→ℝh:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} which beats random guessing in squared error gives a weak agnostic learner. Theorem 3.5 shows that if h:𝒳→[0,1]h:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] satisfies

𝐄[(𝐲−h⁡(𝐱))2]≤𝐄[(𝐲−12)2]−γ.\displaystyle\E[(\mathbf{y}-h(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]\leq\E\left[\left(\mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right]-\gamma.

then 2​h​(x)−12h(x)-1 is a 2​γ2\gamma weak learner. A similar result is proved in the work of [6]. With this characterization in hand, we can rephrase our question to ask when a multiaccurate predictor improves upon random guessing in terms of squared loss. More generally, for what values of α,β\alpha,\beta can one get an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} by post-processing a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate predictor?

When multiaccuracy does not imply agnostic learning.

Motivated by Theorem 3.5, let us first focus on the hypothesis q⁡(x)=2​p​(x)−1q(x)=2p(x)-1 and understand when this fails as a weak learner. To frame this as a geometric question, let q∗​(x)=2​p∗​(x)−1q^{*}(x)=2p^{*}(x)-1. Assume there exists c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} so that ⟨q∗,c⟩=cor⁡(𝐲,c)≥α\langle q^{*},c\rangle=\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c)\geq\alpha. By multiaccuracy, this also means that ⟨q,c⟩≥α\langle q,c\rangle\geq\alpha, since multiaccuracy preserves the projection onto 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For what values of α\alpha is it possible that ⟨q∗,q⟩=0\langle q^{*},q\rangle=0, so that qq is not a β\beta-weak learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C}?

We will show that the answer is α≤1/2\alpha\leq 1/2. Take q,q∗q,q^{*} to be vectors in {±1}n\{\pm 1\}^{n}, so that ⟨q,q∗⟩=0\langle q,q^{*}\rangle=0. Let dHd_{H} denote the normalized Hamming distance in this space. Let c∈{±1}nc\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} be the mid-point of q,q∗q,q^{*} in the Hamming metric. Since dH​(q,c)=dH​(q∗,c)=1/4d_{H}(q,c)=d_{H}(q^{*},c)=1/4, we have ⟨q∗,c⟩=⟨q,c⟩=1/2\langle q^{*},c\rangle=\langle q,c\rangle=1/2. Thus we have a triple of vectors q∗,q,c∈{±1}Nq^{*},q,c\in\{\pm 1\}^{N} such that ⟨q∗,c⟩=⟨q,c⟩=1/2\langle q^{*},c\rangle=\langle q,c\rangle=1/2, whereas ⟨q∗,q⟩=0\langle q^{*},q\rangle=0. Translating this geometric example to a learning setting requires some care, but it conveys the intuition for why 1/21/2 arises as the right threshold.

Theorem 4.1 builds on this to show that there exists a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, a predictor pp and a hypothesis class 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that

  • •

    Opt⁡(𝒞)≥1/2\mathrm{Opt}(\mathcal{C})\geq 1/2,

  • •

    pp is (𝒞,0)(\mathcal{C},0)-multiaccurate,

  • •

    cor⁡(𝐲,k⁡(p))=0\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},k(p))=0 for any k:[0,1]→[−1,1]k:[0,1]\to[-1,1].

The key challenge is ruling out all post-processing functions k⁡(p)k(p), not just 2​p−12p-1. Our construction achieves this by ensuring that for every predicted value vv, 𝐄[𝐲|p⁡(𝐱)=v]=1/2\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})=v]=1/2. Thus the predictor is anti-calibrated in the sense that even conditioned on its predictions, the bit 𝐲\mathbf{y} is uniformly random. This property ensures that no function k⁡(p)k(p) can beat random guessing.

Our construction in Theorem 4.1 makes careful use of the properties of majority and parity functions with respect to the uniform distribution. However, under the additional assumption of the existence of pseudorandom functions, we show in Theorem 4.2 that for any reasonable class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, a multiaccurate predictor cannot in general be post-processed to have non-trivial correlation with the labels, even when Opt⁡(𝒞)\mathrm{Opt}(\mathcal{C}) is large. The key idea is based on making p∗p^{*} and pp both be averages of a function ff from 𝒞\mathcal{C} and a pseudorandom (for 𝒞\mathcal{C}) function gg, but with opposite signs. Thus, p∗−pp^{*}-p is essentially a pseudorandom function, which ensures multiaccuracy. However, even though p∗p^{*} has a high correlation with some c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}, cor⁡(p∗,p)≈0\mathrm{cor}(p^{*},p)\approx 0.

When multiaccuracy implies (restricted) weak agnostic learning.

Complementing this lower bound, Theorem 4.4 shows that pp being 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate implies that 2​p−12p-1 is an (α,2​α−1)(\alpha,2\alpha-1) weak agnostic learner. Note that β>0\beta>0 only when α>1/2\alpha>1/2. This is in contrast with the standard usage of weak learning, where one typically thinks of α\alpha being close to 00, hence we refer to this notion as restricted weak agnostic learning. In the realizable setting where α=1\alpha=1, we get β=1\beta=1.

Intuition for why this is the right bound on β\beta can again be obtained from the geometric setting, where q∗,q,cq^{*},q,c are vectors in {±1}n\{\pm 1\}^{n}. The condition ⟨q,c⟩≥α\langle q,c\rangle\geq\alpha translates to dH​(q,c)≤(1−α)/2d_{H}(q,c)\leq(1-\alpha)/2, and similarly for dH​(q∗,c)d_{H}(q^{*},c). By the triangle inequality, we must have

dH​(q,q∗)≤dH​(q,c)+dH​(q∗,c)≤1−α.d_{H}(q,q^{*})\leq d_{H}(q,c)+d_{H}(q^{*},c)\leq 1-\alpha.

But this means that the correlation is lower bounded by

⟨q,q∗⟩≥1−2​(1−α)=2​α−1.\langle q,q^{*}\rangle\geq 1-2(1-\alpha)=2\alpha-1.

While translating this intuition from the Boolean to the continuous setting is by no means immediate, we show that 2​p−12p-1 is indeed a β=2​α−1\beta=2\alpha-1-weak learner. The key step is to show the following upper bound on the correlation obtainable using any hypothesis in 𝒞\mathcal{C}: if pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate, then

Opt⁡(𝒞)≤𝐄𝒟[p⁡(𝐱)​p∗​(𝐱)+(1−p⁡(𝐱))​(1−p∗​(𝐱))]+τ.\mathrm{Opt}(\mathcal{C})\leq\E_{\mathcal{D}}[p(\mathbf{x})p^{*}(\mathbf{x})+(1-p(\mathbf{x}))(1-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))]+\tau.
Calibrated multiaccuracy gives strong agnostic learning.

We have seen that 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccuracy alone might not give a weak learner. Similarly, calibration by itself need not give a weak learner, since predicting the constant 1/21/2 might be calibrated (if 𝐲\mathbf{y} is balanced). This is a well-known problem with calibration as a standalone notion: its predictions might not be informative.

But we observe that this is the only way that it can fail. In Lemma 4.5, we show that for a calibrated predictor pp,

cor(𝐲,sign(2p−1))≥2𝐄[|p(𝐱)−12|]−2τ.\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},\mathrm{sign}(2p-1))\geq 2\E\left[\left|p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right|\right]-2\tau.

Thus a calibrated predictor that deviates noticeably from random guessing (saying 1/21/2 all the time) gives rise to an agnostic learner. But if we add the assumption that pp is 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate, and that there exists c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} so that cor⁡(𝐲,c⁡(𝐱))≥α\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))\geq\alpha, then pp can no longer predict 1/21/2 all the time. This is proved in Lemma 4.6 which shows that for every c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C},

𝐄[|p⁡(𝐱)−12|]≥12​cor​(𝐲,c⁡(𝐱))−τ.\E\left[\left|p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right|\right]\geq\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))-\tau.

Intuitively, a hypothesis cc that is correlated with 𝐲\mathbf{y} provides a certificate that 𝐲|𝐱\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x} is not uniformly random. A 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate predictor has to capture the correlations with cc accurately, which forces it to deviate from random guessing. Putting these insights together, Theorem 4.7 shows that if pp is both calibrated and 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate, then sign⁡(2​p−1)\mathrm{sign}(2p-1) is a strong agnostic learner.

We note that this result can also be shown using the loss OI technique of [17], where it is applied to show agnostic learning for Boolean function classes 𝒞\mathcal{C} (where correlation coincides with 00-11 loss). But we find the proof above more intuitive as it highlights how multiaccuracy and calibration complement each other.

2.2 Hardcore Sets of Optimal Density

In the context of hardcore sets, we will restrict 𝒞={c:𝒳→{0,1}}\mathcal{C}=\{c:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}\} to be a class of Boolean functions, rather than bounded functions. We will assume that it contains the constant functions 0,1\mathrm{0},\mathrm{1} and is closed under complement. We will use 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} to denote a distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Given a class of functions 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we are interested in studying how well the functions c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} can approximate a target hard Boolean function gg. For δ>0\delta>0, we say that gg is (𝒞,δ)(\mathcal{C},\delta)-hard on 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} if for all c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}, Pr𝒟𝒳[c(𝐱)=g(𝐱)]≤1−δ\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})=g(\mathbf{x})]\leq 1-\delta. We say a distribution is hardcore when δ\delta becomes arbitrarily close to 1/21/2, since this means that it is hard to predict the values of gg much better than random guessing.

A measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a function μ:𝒳→[0,1]\mu:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1], which is not identically 00. It defines a probability distribution μ¯\bar{\mu} by re-weighting 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} by μ\mu. A hardcore measure μ\mu is one which induces a hardcore distribution μ¯\bar{\mu}. Given a measure μ:𝒳→[0,1]\mu:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1] and a base distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the density of μ\mu in 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} is given by

𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)=𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[μ⁡(𝐱)].\mathsf{dns}(\mu)=\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu(\mathbf{x})].

The existence of hardcore measure μ\mu immediately implies that gg is δ=𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)/2\delta=\mathsf{dns}(\mu)/2 hard for 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Impagliazzo’s seminal Hardcore Lemma (IHCL) proves a surprising converse to this statement, provided we assume that gg is δ\delta-hard not just for 𝒞\mathcal{C}, but for a larger class 𝒞′=𝒞t,q\mathcal{C}^{\prime}=\mathcal{C}_{t,q} containing qq oracle gates from 𝒞\mathcal{C} and a total of tt logical gates. Since qq is the more important parameter for us (as 𝒞\mathcal{C} grows in complexity), in this informal discussion we will focus on qq and ignore tt.

Theorem 2.1 (IHCL informal statement, [28, 25]).

There exists q=poly⁡(1/ε,1/δ)q=\poly(1/\varepsilon,1/\delta) such that if g:𝒳→{0,1}g:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\} is (𝒞q,δ)(\mathcal{C}_{q},\delta)-hard on 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, then there is a measure μ\mu satisfying:

  • •

    Hardcore-ness: gg is (𝒞,1/2−O⁡(ϵ))(\mathcal{C},1/2-O(\epsilon))-hard on μ¯\bar{\mu}.

  • •

    Optimal density: 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)=2​δ−o⁡(1)\mathsf{dns}(\mu)=2\delta-o(1).

The density parameter of 2​δ2\delta is optimal, since even a function that computes gg perfectly on the complement of μ\mu will incur error δ\delta from μ\mu. Impagliazzo’s original proof gives density δ\delta [28], the improvement to 2​δ2\delta is due to Holenstein [25]. This is a cornerstone result in the average-case hardness of functions, and has led to a long line of work that explores connections to other areas, such as boosting [35, 13], pseudorandomness [44, 46] and more recently, to multigroup fairness [46, 8]. The last two are most relevant to us, so we discuss them in more detail.

IHCL with density δ\delta from multiaccuracy.

Trevisan, Tulsiani, and Vadhan showed that one can derive Impagliazzo’s Hardcore Lemma from the existence of (what we now call) multiaccurate predictors. We consider the labelled distribution 𝒟g=(𝐱,g⁡(𝐱))\mathcal{D}^{g}=(\mathbf{x},g(\mathbf{x})) and let pp be a (𝒞,ϵ​δ)(\mathcal{C},\epsilon\delta)-multiaccurate predictor pp for gg. Their hardcore measure defined as μ𝖳𝖳𝖵​(x)=|g⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}}(x)=|g(x)-p(x)| is simple and explicit. Their analysis shows 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ𝖳𝖳𝖵)≥δ\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}})\geq\delta, and indeed (while we give a slightly sharper density analysis), one can construct instances where the 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ𝖳𝖳𝖵)=δ+o⁡(1)\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}})=\delta+o(1). The parameter q=O⁡(1/(ε2​δ2))q=O(1/(\varepsilon^{2}\delta^{2})) is governed by the number of calls to a (proper) agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} needed to achieve multiaccuracy with error τ=ε​δ\tau=\varepsilon\delta.

IHCL+⁣+++ from multicalibration.

Recently, Casacuberta, Dwork and Vadhan [8] showed that starting from a multicalibrated predictor, one can derive a stronger and more general version of the IHCL, which they call IHCL+⁣+++. Specifically, they show that given a multicalibrated partition, we can construct hardcore distributions of locally optimal density on each (large enough) piece of the partition. As expected, given that multicalibration is stronger than multiaccuracy, one can recover the original IHCL from IHCL+⁣+++ by “gluing” these local hardcore distributions. This glued distribution is a global 2​δ2\delta-dense hardcore measure.

While this result recovers the optimal hardcore density, the complexity of the class 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} is now considerably larger than in [46], we now get q=O⁡(1/(ε12​δ6))q=O(1/(\varepsilon^{12}\delta^{6})). This increased complexity comes in part because achieving τ\tau-multicalibration requires O⁡(1/τ6)O(1/\tau^{6}) calls to a (strong) agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C}, rather than the O⁡(1/τ2)O(1/\tau^{2}) calls needed for multiaccuracy. We refer the reader to a detailed discussion at the end of Section 5.3.

Our result: IHCL from calibration and weighted multiaccuracy.

We show how to construct hardcore distributions with optimal density 2​δ2\delta as in [8] but with the lower complexity bound of q=O⁡(1/(ε2​δ2))q=O(1/(\varepsilon^{2}\delta^{2})) for 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} as in [46]. Indeed, we give a simple and explicit form for such a measure, starting from a predictor satisfying calibration and a weighted variant of multiaccuracy that we call weighted multiaccuracy. Both calibration and weighted multiaccuracy are implied by multicalibration, so this gives an alternate proof of the optimal density result of [8]. But crucially, the cost of obtaining both these conditions together (by many measures, including oracle calls to the weak learner) is not much more than that of multiaccuracy, which yields a considerably better bound on the parameter qq. To formally state our result, we define weighted multiaccuracy.

We will consider weight functions w:[0,1]→[1,2]w:[0,1]\to[1,2], which assign weights to predictions, as is standard in the calibration literature [19, 7]. While the range [−1,1][-1,1] is more standard, this choice of range is appropriate for hardcore measures. The weight function that will be important for us is

w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p)=1max⁡(p,1−p).w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p)=\frac{1}{\max(p,1-p)}.

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be a distribution on 𝒳×{0,1}\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\} whose marginal on 𝒳\mathcal{X} is 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}. For a weight function w:[0,1]→[1,2]w:[0,1]\to[1,2], we define the (w,𝒞)(w,\mathcal{C})-multiaccuracy error of pp under the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} as

𝖬𝖠𝒟​(w,𝒞,p)=maxc∈𝒞⁡|𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[c⁡(𝐱)​w​(p⁡(𝐱))​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))]|.\mathsf{MA}_{\mathcal{D}}(w,\mathcal{C},p)=\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\Big|\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[c(\mathbf{x})w(p(\mathbf{x}))(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))]\Big|.

Let us contrast weighted multiaccuracy to the notions of multiaccuracy and multicalibration. Multiaccuracy corresponds to the case where w=1w=1, so it is a special case of weighted multiaccuracy. Weighted multiaccuracy specializes the definition of weighted multicalibration from [19] to the case when the weight family consists of a single weight function. Having to focus on a single weight function rather than a family translates to the complexity of computing a predictor satisfying weighted multiaccuracy being similar to that needed for multiaccuracy.

With this definition in place, we can informally state our main result. Recall the distribution 𝒟g=(𝐱,g⁡(𝐱))\mathcal{D}^{g}=(\mathbf{x},g(\mathbf{x})) for 𝐱∼𝒟𝒳\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}.

Theorem 2.2 (IHCL from calibration and weighted multiaccuracy).

Let ε,δ>0\varepsilon,\delta>0, and q=O⁡(1/(ε2​δ2))q=O(1/(\varepsilon^{2}\delta^{2})). Assume that g:𝒳→{0,1}g:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\} is (𝒞q,δ)(\mathcal{C}_{q},\delta)-hard on 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}. Let p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] denote a predictor, and define the measure

μ𝖬𝖺𝗑​(x)=w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p⁡(x))⋅|g⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|=|g⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|max⁡(p⁡(x),1−p⁡(x)).\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}(x)=w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p(x))\cdot|g(x)-p(x)|=\frac{|g(x)-p(x)|}{\max(p(x),1-p(x))}.

Then:

  • •

    Hardcore-ness from weighted multiaccuracy: If 𝖬𝖠𝒟g​(w𝖬𝖺𝗑,𝒞,p)≤ε​𝖽𝗇𝗌​(μ𝖬𝖺𝗑)\mathsf{MA}_{\mathcal{D}^{g}}(w_{\mathsf{Max}},\mathcal{C},p)\leq\varepsilon\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}), then the function gg is (1/2−ε)(1/2-\varepsilon)-hard for 𝒞\mathcal{C} under the distribution μ¯𝖬𝖺𝗑\bar{\mu}_{\mathsf{Max}}.

  • •

    Optimal density from calibration: If pp is τ\tau-calibrated, then 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ𝖬𝖺𝗑)=2​δ−O⁡(τ)\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{Max}})=2\delta-O(\tau).

Here are some key advantages of our result and proof technique:

  • •

    We obtain the optimal density bound of 2​δ2\delta as in [8], but under the assumption of (𝒞q,δ)(\mathcal{C}_{q},\delta) hardness for q=O⁡(1/(ε2​δ2))q=O(1/(\varepsilon^{2}\delta^{2})) as in [46].

  • •

    It clearly delineates the roles played by each of calibration and multiaccuracy in ensuring the resulting measure is a hardcore distribution with optimal density 2​δ2\delta: calibration ensures that the distribution has the optimal density, while weighted multiaccuracy implies the hardcore property.

  • •

    Our technique applies to large class of measures, that we call balanced under calibration measures, which are of the form

    μw​(x)=w⁡(p⁡(x))⋅|g⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|\mu_{w}(x)=w(p(x))\cdot|g(x)-p(x)|

    for a weight function w:[0,1]→[1,2]w:[0,1]\to[1,2] where 1≤w⁡(p)≤w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p)1\leq w(p)\leq w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p). This family includes μ𝖳𝖳𝖵\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}} which corresponds to w=1w=1. We give a tight analysis of the density of all such measures assuming calibration. Our analysis reveals that 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ𝖳𝖳𝖵)\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}}) can sometimes be better than δ\delta.

Along the way, our argument fixes a gap in the gluing argument used to derive the IHCL with density 2​δ2\delta from IHCL+⁣+++ in [8], see the discussion at the end of Section 5.3.66 6 Gluing is straightforward for hardcore sets, but more subtle for hardcore measures.

Improving the density.

We explain at an intuitive level how μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} improves over μ𝖳𝖳𝖵\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}} and gets optimal density. Consider a level set Sv={x:p⁡(x)=v}S_{v}=\{x:p(x)=v\} of the predictor pp and partition it into Sv0S_{v}^{0} and Sv1S_{v}^{1} based on whether g⁡(x)g(x) is 00 or 11. μ𝖳𝖳𝖵\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}} assigns weight 1−v1-v to the points in Sv1S_{v}^{1} and vv to points in Sv0S_{v}^{0}. If the predictor pp is calibrated for this level set, so that Pr⁡[g⁡(𝐱)=1|𝐱∈Sv]=v\Pr[g(\mathbf{x})=1|\mathbf{x}\in S_{v}]=v, then

𝐄[μ𝖳𝖳𝖵​(𝐱)|𝐱∈Sv]=v​Pr​[g⁡(𝐱)=0|𝐱∈Sv]+(1−v)​Pr​[g⁡(𝐱)=1|𝐱∈Sv]=2​v​(1−v).\E[\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}}(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\in S_{v}]=v\Pr[g(\mathbf{x})=0|\mathbf{x}\in S_{v}]+(1-v)\Pr[g(\mathbf{x})=1|\mathbf{x}\in S_{v}]=2v(1-v).

Crucially, the measure gives equal weight v⁡(1−v)v(1-v) to Sv0S_{v}^{0} and Sv1S_{v}^{1}.

Now consider the measure μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}. If v<1/2v<1/2 then μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} assigns weight 11 to points in Sv1S_{v}^{1}, which are in the minority, and constitute a vv fraction of SvS_{v}. It assigns weight v/(1−v)v/(1-v) to points in Sv0S_{v}^{0}, which are in the majority, and constitute a 1−v1-v fraction of SvS_{v}. Overall the weight given to each of Sv0S_{v}^{0} and Sv1S_{v}^{1} is v=min⁡(v,1−v)v=\min(v,1-v). When v>1/2v>1/2, the set Sv1S_{v}^{1} has the majority of points, so μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} assigns weight 11 to points in Sv0S_{v}^{0}, and weighs Sv1S_{v}^{1} so that both have equal weight min⁡(v,1−v)\min(v,1-v).

Why is this a good weighting strategy? Consider the majority predictor p~=𝟏[p≥1/2]\tilde{p}=\mathbf{1}[p\geq 1/2].77 7 This predictor is the best-response if pp is Bayes optimal. μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} assigns weight 11 to the points where p~\tilde{p} is incorrect. The rest of the weights are assigned so that SvS_{v} is balanced, assuming that pp is in fact calibrated. This clearly ensures that p~\tilde{p} is incorrect with probability 1/21/2. We now want to argue both that μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} has good density and that no hypothesis in 𝒞\mathcal{C} can do better than 1/21/2. It is intuitive that if μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} is hard for p~\tilde{p}, which incorporates the distinguishing power of the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, then it should also be hard for 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

The analysis of the density follows that of [8], with the added observation that this part only requires global calibration of pp, not multicalibration. We assume that p~∈𝒞q\tilde{p}\in\mathcal{C}_{q}, so it must have error at least δ\delta. But the error of p~\tilde{p} is exactly 𝐄[min⁡(p⁡(𝐱),1−p⁡(𝐱))]\E[\min(p(\mathbf{x}),1-p(\mathbf{x}))]. Whereas we have

𝖽𝗇𝗌(μ𝖬𝖺𝗑)=2𝐄[min(p(𝐱)),1−p(𝐱))],\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{Max}})=2\E[\min(p(\mathbf{x})),1-p(\mathbf{x}))],

so we get that 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ𝖬𝖺𝗑)≥2​δ\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{Max}})\geq 2\delta. A similar analysis of μ𝖳𝖳𝖵\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}} under the assumption of calibration shows

𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ𝖳𝖳𝖵)=𝐄[2​p​(𝐱)​(1−p⁡(𝐱))].\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}})=\E[2p(\mathbf{x})(1-p(\mathbf{x}))].

This is at least δ\delta, since 2​v​(1−v)≥min⁡(v,1−v)2v(1-v)\geq\min(v,1-v) for v∈[0,1]v\in[0,1]. If p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}) is far from 1/21/2 with reasonable probability, then it gives a better bound than δ\delta.

It remains to argue that the measure μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} is hardcore. In Lemma 5.8 we present a characterization of the prediction advantage of 𝒞\mathcal{C} under the distribution μ¯w\bar{\mu}_{w} in terms of the (w,𝒞)(w,\mathcal{C})-weighted multiaccuracy error of pp under the distribution 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g}. This tells us that if the multiaccuracy error is τ\tau, then the prediction advantage under μ¯w\bar{\mu}_{w} is τ/𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μw)\tau/\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{w}). This proof technique is different from [8, Lemma 2.17] who show that if a function is indistinguishable from a constant function vv to 𝒞\mathcal{C} on each level set SvS_{v}, then then one can obtain a hardcore set of density 2​min⁡(v,1−v)2\min(v,1-v) within SvS_{v}. The required indistinguishability holds for every level set by the assumption of multicalibration. Our result can be seen as a simplification and extension of the hardness result in [46] to weighted measures.

Note that calibrated multiaccuracy does not give the stronger IHCL+⁣+++ theorem proved in [8]; indeed that seems to require the full power of multicalibration. Also, the min-max based proof of Nisan as cited in [28] and the boosting-based proof of [35] give qq which grows as O⁡(log⁡(1/δ))O(\log(1/\delta)), but they do not get optimal density. The 1/ε21/\varepsilon^{2} dependence on ε\varepsilon was recently showed to be necessary by [4].

2.3 Multiaccuracy and Restricted Weak Agnostic Learning

As discussed earlier and shown in Theorem 4.4, any pp that is multiaccurate for 𝒞\mathcal{C} can be viewed as a (2​α−1)(2\alpha-1)-weak learner when α>1/2\alpha>1/2. Thus multiaccuracy by itself only yields a restricted form of (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learning, giving non-trivial learners only for α>1/2\alpha>1/2. Syntactically, the task of (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak learning gets harder as α\alpha decreases, since this corresponds to detecting lower correlation, and as β\beta increases, since this corresponds to learning a better hypothesis.

The agnostic boosting results of [30, 13] tell us that increasing β\beta does not necessarily result in harder learning problems, provided weak learners exist for arbitrarily small values of α\alpha. They show that an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) weak learner implies a (γ,γ−α)(\gamma,\gamma-\alpha) weak learner for all γ>α\gamma>\alpha. This will improve on the trivial (γ,β)(\gamma,\beta) weak learner provided γ>α+β\gamma>\alpha+\beta. In particular, this result shows that if weak agnostic learning is possible for arbitrarily small values of α\alpha, then strong agnostic learning is possible.

The following natural questions arise:

  • •

    Boosting the α\alpha parameter: Given an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak learner, can one construct an (α′,β′)(\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime})-weak learner for α′<α\alpha^{\prime}<\alpha? If this is possible, it would give a boosting result for the α\alpha parameter in restricted weak agnostic learning.

  • •

    Multiaccuracy from Restricted Weak Agnostic Learning: Given an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C}, can one get a (𝒞,α′)(\mathcal{C},\alpha^{\prime})-multiaccuracy for α′<α\alpha^{\prime}<\alpha? [24] already show how to get α′=α\alpha^{\prime}=\alpha.

The questions are related since if we can boost the α\alpha parameter, we can also reduce multiaccuracy error. We answer both questions in the negative, but the second comes with some loss in parameters.

The α\alpha-parameter for Restricted Weak Agnostic Learning cannot be boosted.

We make a standard cryptographic assumption that pseudorandom functions cannot be distinguished from random functions with non-negligible advantage by efficient algorithms;88 8 In fact, these algorithms could be super-polynomial depending on how strong an assumption one is willing to make. this, for example, follows from the existence of one-way functions [15]. The result below is an informal version of Theorem 6.5 (Parts (i) and (ii)).

Theorem 2.3.

Assuming the existence of a pseudorandom family of functions, there exists a concept class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, such that, for every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), there is a marginal distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, so that,

  • •

    𝒞\mathcal{C} is efficiently (α+ϵ,α)(\alpha+\epsilon,\alpha)-weak agnostically learnable under any 𝒟\mathcal{D} with marginal 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}},

  • •

    𝒞\mathcal{C} is not efficiently (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak learnable for distributions 𝒟\mathcal{D} with marginal 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}.

The domain 𝒳\mathcal{X} is divided into two disjoint parts EE and FF; each hypothesis consists of a pseudorandom function frf_{r} and its key rr. The key rr is represented in EE and the hypothesis on FF is just the pseudorandom function frf_{r}. In the absence of noise, this class is not hard to learn, as the key can be constructed from the examples in EE and then the function frf_{r} can be identified exactly; on the other hand, if there is sufficient noise to make the labels on EE completely random, then the learning problem becomes equivalent to learning pseudorandom functions. In order to get a tight gap, instead of representing rr directly in EE, we use a representation using error-correcting codes. In particular, if we use list-decodable codes that can tolerate error up to slightly less than 1/21/2 (e.g.[22]), then we obtain the tight characterization given above.

Multiaccuracy from Restricted Weak Agnostic Learning.

As discussed earlier, [24] already show that access to an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learning algorithm is sufficient for constructing a predictor pp that is α\alpha-multicalibrated for 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Using the same construction as in Theorem 2.3, we show (Theorem 6.5, Part (iii)) that it is not possible to get τ\tau-multiaccuracy for τ<α/2−ε\tau<\alpha/2-\varepsilon using only an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learning algorithm. Intuitively this factor of 22 comes as cor(𝐲,c)−cor(p,c)=2𝐄[c(𝐱)(𝐲−p(𝐱))]\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c)-\mathrm{cor}(p,c)=2\E[c(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))];99 9 As an aside, we note that even if we only had (1,β)(1,\beta)-weak learning, corresponding to realizable weak learning, achieving 1/21/2 multiaccuracy is straightforward by setting p⁡(𝐱)=1/2p(\mathbf{x})=1/2 for all 𝐱\mathbf{x}. thus if cor⁡(𝐲,c)=α+ε\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c)=\alpha+\varepsilon, we get that cor⁡(p,c)≥ε\mathrm{cor}(p,c)\geq\varepsilon. As in the Theorem 2.3 described above, the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} is chosen so that 𝐲\mathbf{y} is random noise on EE, so learning directly with access to the labels is as hard as learning a pseudorandom function. On the other hand, depending on whether the non-negligible correlation cor⁡(p,c)≥ε\mathrm{cor}(p,c)\geq\varepsilon comes from EE or FF: we can either decode the key rr and hence learn frf_{r}, or we have that pp itself has non-negligible correlation with the pseudorandom function frf_{r}. In either case, we violate the cryptographic assumption.

The spectrum of weak agnostic learning.

Figure 2 summarizes the spectrum of what we know about the feasibility of weak agnostic learning. The region of interest is β≤α\beta\leq\alpha. Going right or down, the problem becomes easier, whereas going up or left is harder. Green indicates regions that are known to be easy in general (under the right learning assumptions), while Red indicates regions that are hard (in the worst case over all 𝒞\mathcal{C}).

  • •

    The Orange line bounds the region that is feasible if we have access to a (𝒞,0)(\mathcal{C},0)-multiaccurate predictor. This follows from our Theorem 4.4. If we also assume calibration, the entire region β≤α\beta\leq\alpha is feasible.

  • •

    The Blue line with slope 11 follows from the boosting results of [30, 13].

  • •

    The Red region indicates that there is no black-box reduction from (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) weak agnostic learning to (α−ε,β′)(\alpha-\varepsilon,\beta^{\prime}) weak agnostic learning, assuming the existence of one-way functions. This follows from our Theorem 6.5.

3 Notation & Preliminaries

We introduce the notation and background that is used throughout the paper in this section. Further notation and background is introduced in sections as required. We consider the setting of supervised learning where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a distribution on pairs (𝐱,𝐲)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) where 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a feature vector from a space 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝐲∈{0,1}\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\} is a label. We denote by 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} the marginal distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Boldface typically refers to random variables.

A predictor is a function p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] which associates every feature vector 𝐱\mathbf{x} with an (estimated) probability p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}) that the label 𝐲|𝐱\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x} is 11. The Bayes optimal predictor is given by p∗​(𝐱)=𝐄[𝐲|𝐱]p^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\E[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}], and represents the ground truth.

3.1 Agnostic Learning

We consider a hypothesis class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, where each c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} is a function from 𝒳→[−1,1]\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[-1,1].

Definition 3.1.

The correlation of a function c:𝒳→[−1,1]c:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[-1,1] with respect to a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} over 𝒳×{0,1}\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\}, is defined as cor𝒟​(𝐲,c)=𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[(2​𝐲−1)​c​(𝐱)]\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c)=\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[(2\mathbf{y}-1)c(\mathbf{x})].

The transformation 𝐲→2​𝐲−1\mathbf{y}\to 2\mathbf{y}-1 maps {0,1}\{0,1\} to {±1}\{\pm 1\}. Hence the correlation measures the correlation between cc and {±1}\{\pm 1\} labels associated with 𝐲\mathbf{y}. Given a predictor p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1], we will use the function 2​p−12p-1 which has range [−1,1][-1,1] when considering correlation. The notion of weak agnostic learning we use is along the lines of that defined in [31, 30, 13].

Definition 3.2 (Weak agnostic learner).

For α≥β>0\alpha\geq\beta>0, an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} with marginal distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} is an algorithm that when given access to random examples from any 𝒟\mathcal{D} whose marginal over 𝒳\mathcal{X} is 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, if there exists c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} such that

cor𝒟​(𝐲,c⁡(𝐱))≥α,\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))\geq\alpha,

returns a hypothesis hh such that with probability at least 0.990.99,1010 10 As the algorithm has access to random examples, for any ρ>0\rho>0, we can always boost the success probability to guarantee that for any 0<τ≤β0<\tau\leq\beta, the output of the algorithm will satisfy, with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho, cor𝒟​(𝐲,h⁡(𝐱))≥β−τ\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},h(\mathbf{x}))\geq\beta-\tau. The increase in sample complexity and runtime bounded by a factor that is polynomial in 1/τ,log⁡(1/ρ)1/\tau,\log(1/\rho).

cor𝒟​(𝐲,h⁡(𝐱))≥β.\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},h(\mathbf{x}))\geq\beta.

We further say that hh is a proper weak agnostic learner if h∈𝒞h\in\mathcal{C}, and improper otherwise.

Weak agnostic learning is a broad definition that covers a wide range of learners.

  • •

    A weak agnostic learner gets more powerful as α\alpha decreases and β\beta increases. In other words, an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak learner implies an (α′,β′)(\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime})-weak learner for α′≥α\alpha^{\prime}\geq\alpha and β′≤β\beta^{\prime}\leq\beta.

  • •

    The most powerful weak agnostic learner is one that can handle any positive α\alpha, and has β=poly⁡(α)\beta=\poly(\alpha). Colloquially weak agnostic learning is sometimes used to refer to this setting (where α\alpha approaches 00), but as results on agnostic boosting show [30, 13], this is in fact equivalent to strong agnostic learning.1111 11 We would expect the sample complexity and computational complexity to grow as an (ideally polynomial) function of 1/β1/\beta.

  • •

    Intuitively, weak agnostic learning gets easier as α\alpha increases. The least powerful notion is a learner that only works in the realizable case when α=1\alpha=1.

Definition 3.3 (Strong agnostic learner).

For a hypothesis class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, a strong agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} under the marginal distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} is an algorithm that given any ε>0\varepsilon>0 as the target error parameter and random samples from any 𝒟\mathcal{D} with marginal distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} returns a hypothesis h:𝒳→[−1,1]h:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1] such that with probability at least 0.990.99,

cor𝒟​(𝐲,h⁡(𝐱))≥maxc∈𝒞⁡cor𝒟​(𝐲,c⁡(𝐱))−ε.\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},h(\mathbf{x}))\geq\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))-\varepsilon.

The failure probability can be made arbitrarily small using standard techniques. A strong agnostic learner yields an (α,α−ε)(\alpha,\alpha-\varepsilon) weak agnostic learner for all ε>0\varepsilon>0 and α∈(ε,1]\alpha\in(\varepsilon,1].

Agnostic boosting [30, 13] tells us that strong agnostic learning reduces to weak agnostic learning for small α\alpha. The result below follows by appealing to Theorem 1 of [30]. In particular, it is straightforward to see that an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) weak learner as in Definition 3.2 is an (α​β,β,0.01)(\alpha\beta,\beta,0.01) weak learner as defined in their work.

Theorem 3.4 (Agnostic Boosting, [30]).

An (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} can be boosted to a strong agnostic learner under the same marginal distribution on 𝒳\mathcal{X} to obtain a hypothesis hh that satisfies with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho,

cor𝒟​(𝐲,h⁡(𝐱))≥maxc∈𝒞⁡cor𝒟​(𝐲,c⁡(𝐱))−α−ε\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},h(\mathbf{x}))\geq\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))-\alpha-\varepsilon

for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, using poly⁡(1/ε,1/β,1/ρ)\poly(1/\varepsilon,1/\beta,1/\rho) calls to the weak agnostic learner.

We can interpret this result as follows: provided we have an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for some α\alpha, then for any α′≥α\alpha^{\prime}\geq\alpha, we can obtain an (α′,α′−α−ϵ)(\alpha^{\prime},\alpha^{\prime}-\alpha-\epsilon)-weak agnostic learner for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0; furthermore such a learner can be obtained using at most poly⁡(1/ϵ,1/β,1/ρ)\poly(1/\epsilon,1/\beta,1/\rho) calls to the (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner. In particular, if we can design an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for any α>0\alpha>0, then we obtain (improper) strong agnostic learning.

Weak Learning as Squared Loss Minimization

We observe that weak learning is essentially equivalent to non-trivial squared loss minimization that beats random guessing. This observation is not entirely new, but will help elucidate several of our results.

Assume that we have a function h:𝒳→[−1,1]h:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1] so that cor⁡(𝐲,h⁡(𝐱))=𝐄[h⁡(𝐱)​(2​𝐲−1)]≥β\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},h(\mathbf{x}))=\E[h(\mathbf{x})(2\mathbf{y}-1)]\geq\beta. For instance, hh could be the output of an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner. Then [24] shows that the update p⁡(𝐱)=(1+β​h​(𝐱))/2p(\mathbf{x})=(1+\beta h(\mathbf{x}))/2 satisfies

𝐄[(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))2]≤𝐄[(𝐲−12)2]−3​β24.\displaystyle\E[(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]\leq\E\left[\left(\mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right]-\frac{3\beta^{2}}{4}.

In other words, weak agnostic learning enables non-trivial squared loss minimization, when compared to random guessing.

In the other direction, we show that any function h:𝒳→ℝh:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} which beats random guessing in squared error gives a weak agnostic learner. A similar result is proved in the work of [6].

Theorem 3.5.

Let h:𝒳→ℝh:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} satisfy

𝐄[(𝐲−h⁡(𝐱))2]≤𝐄[(𝐲−12)2]−γ.\displaystyle\E[(\mathbf{y}-h(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]\leq\E\left[\left(\mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right]-\gamma.

Define the function h¯\bar{h} which truncates hh to [0,1][0,1], and let g⁡(x)=2​h¯​(x)−1∈[−1,1]g(x)=2\bar{h}(x)-1\in[-1,1]. Then cor⁡(𝐲,g⁡(𝐱))≥2​γ\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},g(\mathbf{x}))\geq 2\gamma.

Proof.

Since truncation to the range [0,1][0,1] only reduces the squared loss, we have

𝐄[(𝐲−h¯​(𝐱))2]≤𝐄[(𝐲−12)2]−γ.\displaystyle\E[(\mathbf{y}-\bar{h}(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]\leq\E\left[\left(\mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right]-\gamma. (1)

We can write

𝐄[(2​𝐲−2​h¯​(𝐱))2]\displaystyle\E[(2\mathbf{y}-2\bar{h}(\mathbf{x}))^{2}] =𝐄[(2​𝐲−1−g⁡(x))2]\displaystyle=\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1-g(x))^{2}]
=𝐄[(2𝐲−1)2]−2𝐄[g(𝐱)(2𝐲−1)]+𝐄[g(𝐱)2].\displaystyle=\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)^{2}]-2\E[g(\mathbf{x})(2\mathbf{y}-1)]+\E[g(\mathbf{x})^{2}].

Rearranging terms, we get

𝐄[g​(𝐱)​(2​𝐲−1)]\displaystyle\E[g(\mathbf{x})(2\mathbf{y}-1)] =12​(𝐄[(2​𝐲−1)2]−𝐄[(2​𝐲−2​h¯​(𝐱))2]+𝐄[g​(𝐱)2])\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)^{2}]-\E[(2\mathbf{y}-2\bar{h}(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]+\E[g(\mathbf{x})^{2}]\right)
≥2​(𝐄[(𝐲−12)2]−𝐄[(𝐲−h¯​(𝐱))2])\displaystyle\geq 2\left(\E\left[\left(\mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right]-\E[(\mathbf{y}-\bar{h}(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]\right)
≥2​γ.\displaystyle\geq 2\gamma.

where we use Equation (1). The claim follows since the LHS is equal to cor⁡(𝐲,g⁡(𝐱))\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},g(\mathbf{x})). ∎

In essence, these results tell us that weak agnostic learning is equivalent to learning a predictor whose squared loss beats random guessing. This is reminiscent of the result of [36] who show that weak agnostic learning for a class 𝒞\mathcal{C} is equivalent to distinguishing labelled distributions where cor⁡(𝐲,c⁡(𝐱))≥α\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))\geq\alpha for some hypothesis c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} from the distribution where 𝐲\mathbf{y} consists of random bits (since in the latter case, random guessing is in fact optimal).

3.2 Multigroup Fairness Notions

We start by recalling the basic notions of accuracy in expectation and calibration.

Accuracy in expectation and calibration.

A predictor pp is (perfectly) accurate in expectation if 𝐄[𝐲]=𝐄[p⁡(𝐱)]\E[\mathbf{y}]=\E[p(\mathbf{x})]. Accordingly, we define the expected accuracy error of a predictor as

𝖤𝖠𝖤(p)=|𝐄[𝐲]−𝐄[p(𝐱)]|.\displaystyle\mathsf{EAE}(p)=\Bigl\lvert\E[\mathbf{y}]-\E[p(\mathbf{x})]\Bigr\rvert. (2)

A predictor pp is calibrated if 𝐄[𝐲|p⁡(𝐱)]=p⁡(𝐱)\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]=p(\mathbf{x}) (we assume p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}) has a discrete range for simplicity). Accordingly, we define the expected calibration error of a predictor as

𝖤𝖢𝖤(p)=𝐄[|𝐄[𝐲|p(𝐱)]−p(𝐱)|].\displaystyle\mathsf{ECE}(p)=\E\left[\Bigl\lvert\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]-p(\mathbf{x})\Bigr\rvert\right]. (3)

We say pp is τ\tau-calibrated under 𝒟\mathcal{D} if 𝖤𝖢𝖤⁡(p,𝒟)≤τ\mathsf{ECE}(p,\mathcal{D})\leq\tau. The following characterization of 𝖤𝖢𝖤\mathsf{ECE} in terms of bounded auditing functions is standard (see e.g [19]).

𝖤𝖢𝖤(p,𝒟)=maxv:[0,1]→[−1,1]𝐄𝒟[v(p(x))(y−p(x))].\displaystyle\mathsf{ECE}(p,\mathcal{D})=\max_{v:[0,1]\to[-1,1]}\E_{\mathcal{D}}[v(p(x))(y-p(x))]. (4)

We now define the notions of multiaccuracy [46, 24], calibration [9], calibrated multiaccuracy [17] and multicalibration [24]. In this subsection, we assume that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a class of functions, c:𝒳→{0,1}c:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\}; this is more natural as these functions are viewed as group membership.

Definition 3.6.

We say that a predictor pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate for a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} if

maxc∈𝒞|𝐄𝒟[c⁡(𝐱)​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))]|≤τ.\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\Bigl\lvert\E_{\mathcal{D}}[c(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))]\Bigr\rvert\leq\tau.

We say the predictor is τ\tau-calibrated for 𝒟\mathcal{D} if

𝐄[|𝐄[𝐲|p(𝐱)]−p(𝐱)]|]≤τ.\E[|\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]-p(\mathbf{x})]|]\leq\tau.

We say that pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate and calibrated if it is both (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate and τ\tau-calibrated. Further, we say that pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multicalibrated if

maxc∈𝒞⁡𝐄[|c⁡(𝐱)​(𝐄[𝐲|p⁡(𝐱)]−p⁡(𝐱))|]≤τ.\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\E[|c(\mathbf{x})(\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]-p(\mathbf{x}))|]\leq\tau.

We will assume that the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} always contains the constant 𝟏\mathbf{1} function; note that this is simply requiring that (approximate) accuracy in expectation hold. For a function c:𝒳→{0,1}c:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}, let c¯:X→[−1,1]\bar{c}:X\to[-1,1] denote the function, c¯​(𝐱)=2​c​(𝐱)−1\bar{c}(\mathbf{x})=2c(\mathbf{x})-1. Then if pp satisfies (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccuracy for distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we have

|𝐄𝒟[c¯(𝐱)(𝐲−p(𝐱))]|\displaystyle\Bigl\lvert\E_{\mathcal{D}}[\bar{c}(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))]\Bigr\rvert =|𝐄𝒟[(2c(𝐱)−1)(𝐲−p∗(𝐱))]|\displaystyle=\Bigl\lvert\E_{\mathcal{D}}[(2c(\mathbf{x})-1)(\mathbf{y}-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))]\Bigr\rvert
≤2|𝐄𝒟[c(𝐱)(𝐲−p∗(𝐱)]|+|𝐄𝒟[1⋅(𝐲−p∗(𝐱))]|\displaystyle\leq 2\Bigl\lvert\E_{\mathcal{D}}[c(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-p^{*}(\mathbf{x})]\Bigr\rvert+\Bigl\lvert\E_{\mathcal{D}}[1\cdot(\mathbf{y}-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))]\Bigr\rvert
≤3​τ.\displaystyle\leq 3\tau.

Thus, if 𝒞¯\bar{\mathcal{C}} is the hypothesis class representing the {±1}\{\pm 1\} versions of the functions in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, then pp is (𝒞¯,3​τ)(\bar{\mathcal{C}},3\tau)-multiaccurate with respect to 𝒟\mathcal{D} as per Definition 3.6. As a result, we will move freely between the {0,1}\{0,1\} and {±1}\{\pm 1\} versions of functions.

Calibrated multiaccuracy is an intermediate notion between multiaccuracy and multicalibration; see [17] for more details. For any τ>0\tau>0, it is known that having an (τ,poly⁡(τ))(\tau,\poly(\tau))-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} is sufficient to learn a predictor that (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multicalibrated [24, 18]. Indeed, if one only wants (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccuracy, then there is a simple algorithm which performs least-squares regression over 𝒞\mathcal{C} via gradient descent, using the weak agnostic learner at each stage to find a gradient update [17]. One could ask if the reverse connection holds: is having an algorithm that learns a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccurate predictor sufficient to get a weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C}? We provide some answers to this question in Section 4.

4 From Multiaccuracy to Agnostic Learning

As discussed in Section 3, it is known that having a (τ,poly⁡(τ))(\tau,\poly(\tau))-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} is sufficient learn a predictor that is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multicalibrated with poly⁡(1/τ)\poly(1/\tau) oracle calls to the weak learner [24, 18]. Indeed, if one only wants (𝒞,poly⁡(τ))(\mathcal{C},\poly(\tau))-multiaccuracy, there is a simpler algorithm which performs least-squares regression over 𝒞\mathcal{C} via gradient descent, using the weak agnostic learner at each stage to find a gradient update [17]. Here we consider the reverse question: does a (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate predictor yield some form of agnostic learning?

4.1 Multiaccuracy and Weak Agnostic Learning

Our first theorem shows that a multiaccurate predictor pp by itself cannot be transformed into even a weak agnostic learner, even when there exists a function in 𝒞\mathcal{C} that has cor𝒟​(𝐲,c)=1/2\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c)=1/2.

Theorem 4.1.

There exists a class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} on 𝒳×{0,1}\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\}, and a predictor p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] such that

  • •

    pp is (𝒞,0)(\mathcal{C},0)-multiaccurate.

  • •

    For any k:[0,1]→[−1,1]k:[0,1]\to[-1,1], k⁡(p)k(p) is not a (1/2,β)(1/2,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} for any β>0\beta>0.

Proof.

We consider the uniform distribution on the domain {±1}n\{\pm 1\}^{n}. Let 𝐄[𝐲|𝐱]=p∗​(𝐱)\E[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}]=p^{*}(\mathbf{x}) for p∗:{±1}n→[0,1]p^{*}:\{\pm 1\}^{n}\to[0,1]. Every such function specifies a joint distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} on {±1}n×{0,1}\{\pm 1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}.

Let 𝒞={c:{±1}n−1→[−1,1]}\mathcal{C}=\{c:\{\pm 1\}^{n-1}\to[-1,1]\} be the set of all functions of the first n−1n-1 bits. Now define the predictor pp as p⁡(x1,…,xn)=p∗​(x1,…,xn−1,−xn)p(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=p^{*}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1},-x_{n}). If we write the multilinear expansion of p∗p^{*} as

p∗​(x1,…,xn)=p0∗​(x1,…,xn−1)+xn​p1∗​(x1,…,xn−1)\displaystyle p^{*}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=p^{*}_{0}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1})+x_{n}p^{*}_{1}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1})

then we have

p⁡(x1,…,xn)\displaystyle p(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) =p0∗​(x1,…,xn−1)−xn​p1∗​(x1,…,xn−1)\displaystyle=p^{*}_{0}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1})-x_{n}p^{*}_{1}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1})
hence​p∗​(x)−p⁡(x)\displaystyle\text{hence}\ p^{*}(x)-p(x) =2​xn​p1∗​(x1,…,xn−1)\displaystyle=2x_{n}p^{*}_{1}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1})

It follows that for any function c⁡(x1,…,xn−1)c(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}) of the first n−1n-1 bits,

𝐄[c⁡(𝐱)​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))]=𝐄[c⁡(𝐱)​(p∗​(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱))]=𝐄[c⁡(𝐱)​2​𝐱n​p1∗​(𝐱)]=0\displaystyle\E[c(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))]=\E[c(\mathbf{x})(p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x}))]=\E[c(\mathbf{x})2\mathbf{x}_{n}p^{*}_{1}(\mathbf{x})]=0

since both cc and p1∗p^{*}_{1} only depend on the first n−1n-1 bits. So pp is (𝒞,0)(\mathcal{C},0)-multiaccurate for 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

We now construct examples of distributions where k⁡(p)k(p) does not give non-trivial correlation for any k:[0,1]→[−1,1]k:[0,1]\to[-1,1]. Define MAJ:{±1}3→{0,1}\mathrm{MAJ}:\{\pm 1\}^{3}\to\{0,1\} as

MAJ⁡(x1,x2,x3)={1x1+x2+x3>00otherwise\mathrm{MAJ}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=\begin{cases}1&x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}>0\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

For any pair of distinct indices i,j∈[n−1]i,j\in[n-1] let us denote the distribution 𝒟i​j\mathcal{D}_{ij} where the marginal over 𝐱\mathbf{x} is uniform and the conditional label distribution 𝐲|𝐱\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x} is defined by the Bayes optimal predictor

pi​j∗​(𝐱)=MAJ⁡(xi,xj,xn).p^{*}_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=\mathrm{MAJ}(x_{i},x_{j},x_{n}).

Then consider the predictor

pi​j​(𝐱)=MAJ⁡(xi,xj,−xn).p_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=\mathrm{MAJ}(x_{i},x_{j},-x_{n}).

The key observation is that while pi​jp_{ij} is multiaccurate, its predictions do not tell us much about pi​j∗p^{*}_{ij}. Indeed we have

Pr[pi​j∗(𝐱)=pi​j(𝐱)]=Pr[𝐱i=𝐱j]=12.\Pr[p^{*}_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=p_{ij}(\mathbf{x})]=\Pr[\mathbf{x}_{i}=\mathbf{x}_{j}]=\frac{1}{2}.
Pr[pi​j∗(𝐱)≠pi​j(𝐱)]=Pr[𝐱i≠𝐱j]=12.\Pr[p^{*}_{ij}(\mathbf{x})\neq p_{ij}(\mathbf{x})]=\Pr[\mathbf{x}_{i}\neq\mathbf{x}_{j}]=\frac{1}{2}.

A simple analysis shows that

𝐄[(2​𝐲−1)|pij​(𝐱)=0]\displaystyle\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)|p_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=0] =𝐄[(2​𝐲−1)|pij​(𝐱)=1]=0.\displaystyle=\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)|p_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=1]=0. (5)

Hence for any k:[0,1]→[−1,1]k:[0,1]\to[-1,1],

cor𝒟i​j​(𝐲,k∘pi​j​(𝐱))\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}_{ij}}(\mathbf{y},k\circ p_{ij}(\mathbf{x})) =k⁡(0)2𝐄[(2𝐲−1)|pij(𝐱)=0]+k⁡(1)2𝐄[(2𝐲−1)|pij(𝐱)=1]=0.\displaystyle=\frac{k(0)}{2}\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)|p_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=0]+\frac{k(1)}{2}\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)|p_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=1]=0.

Although no function k∘pi​jk\circ p_{ij} has non-zero correlation with pi​j∗p^{*}_{ij}, the dictator function ci∈𝒞c_{i}\in\mathcal{C} defined as ci​(𝐱)=xic_{i}(\mathbf{x})=x_{i} has correlation 1/21/2 since

𝐄[(2​𝐲−1)​xi|xi=1]\displaystyle\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)x_{i}|x_{i}=1] =𝐄[(2​𝐲−1)​xi|xi=−1]=34−14=12.\displaystyle=\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)x_{i}|x_{i}=-1]=\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{2}.
Thus,
cor𝒟i​j​(𝐲,ci​(𝐱))\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}_{ij}}(\mathbf{y},c_{i}(\mathbf{x})) =12𝐄[(2𝐲−1)xi|xi=1]+12𝐄[(2𝐲−1)xi|xi=−1]=12.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)x_{i}|x_{i}=1]+\frac{1}{2}\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)x_{i}|x_{i}=-1]=\frac{1}{2}.

This proves that a black-box reduction from (C,0)(C,0)-multiaccuracy cannot give a (1/2,β)(1/2,\beta) weak agnostic learner for any β>0\beta>0. ∎

We observe that Eqn. 5 in the proof above shows that pp is maximally anti-calibrated, in the sense that 𝐄[𝐲|p⁡(𝐱)=v]=1/2\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})=v]=1/2 for any vv in the range of pp. Such a predictor is clearly no better than random guessing in terms of squared loss. This construction also provides a counterpoint to Lemma 4.5 which shows that any non-trivial calibration enforces some correlation with the target 𝐲\mathbf{y}.

Our next result shows that assuming the existence of pseudorandom functions that fool the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, a very general result can be established — namely that, in general, no post-processing of a multiaccurate predictor yields a weak agnostic learner.

Theorem 4.2.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a hypothesis class of functions with range {−1,1}\{-1,1\} and 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} be a distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Suppose there exists an efficiently computable function g:𝒳→{0,1}g:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\} such that,

∀c∈𝒞,∀v∈{−1,1},|Pr𝒟𝒳⁡[g⁡(𝐱)=1|c⁡(𝐱)=v]−12|≤τ2.\forall c\in\mathcal{C},\forall v\in\{-1,1\},\quad\left|\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[g(\mathbf{x})=1|c(\mathbf{x})=v]-\frac{1}{2}\right|\leq\frac{\tau}{2}.

Then there exists a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} over 𝒳×{0,1}\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\} with the marginal distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X} being 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, and an efficiently computable predictor p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1] such that,

  • •

    pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate for 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

  • •

    For any k:[0,1]→[−1,1]k:[0,1]\rightarrow[-1,1], k⁡(p)k(p) is not a (q−τ,β)(q-\tau,\beta) agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} for any β>τ\beta>\tau, where

    q=maxc∈C{min{Pr𝒟𝒳[c(𝐱)=1],Pr𝒟𝒳[c(𝐱)=−1]}}.q=\max_{c\in C}\left\{\min\{\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})=1],\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})=-1]\}\right\}.
Proof.

Fix some f∈𝒞f\in\mathcal{C} and let q=Pr𝒟𝒳[f(𝐱)=1]q=\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[f(\mathbf{x})=1]. Assume without loss of generality that 0<q≤120<q\leq\frac{1}{2}. Let f^:𝒳→{−1,1}\widehat{f}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{-1,1\} be a (randomized) function such that

f^​(x)\displaystyle\widehat{f}(x) ={1if ​f​(x)=1,1with probability ​1−2​q2​(1−q)​ if ​f​(x)=−1,−1with probability ​12​(1−q)​ if ​f​(x)=−1.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }f(x)=1,\\ 1&\text{with probability }\frac{1-2q}{2(1-q)}\text{ if }f(x)=-1,\\ -1&\text{with probability }\frac{1}{2(1-q)}\text{ if }f(x)=-1.\end{cases}

We have defined f^\widehat{f} to be a ±1\pm 1-valued function that is a balanced version of ff; in particular, Pr𝒟𝒳[f^(𝐱)=1]=12\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\widehat{f}(\mathbf{x})=1]=\frac{1}{2}. Note that

𝐄𝒟𝒳[f⁡(𝐱)​f^​(𝐱)]\displaystyle\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[f(\mathbf{x})\widehat{f}(\mathbf{x})] =𝐄𝒟𝒳[f⁡(𝐱)​f^​(𝐱)|f⁡(𝐱)=1]⋅q+𝐄𝒟𝒳[f⁡(𝐱)​f^​(𝐱)|f⁡(𝐱)=−1]⋅(1−q)=2​q.\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[f(\mathbf{x})\widehat{f}(\mathbf{x})|f(\mathbf{x})=1]\cdot q+\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[f(\mathbf{x})\widehat{f}(\mathbf{x})|f(\mathbf{x})=-1]\cdot(1-q)=2q. (6)

Let g^:𝒳→{−1,1}\widehat{g}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{-1,1\} be defined as the ±1\pm 1-valued version of gg, i.e. g^​(x)=2​g​(x)−1\widehat{g}(x)=2g(x)-1. Define the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} with the marginal distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} over 𝒳\mathcal{X} such that,

𝐄[𝐲|𝐱]=p∗​(𝐱)=2+f^​(𝐱)+g^​(𝐱)4.\E[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}]=p^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{2+\widehat{f}(\mathbf{x})+\widehat{g}(\mathbf{x})}{4}.

Finally, define a predictor p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1] as

p⁡(x)=2+f^​(x)−g^​(x)4.p(x)=\frac{2+\widehat{f}(x)-\widehat{g}(x)}{4}.

In order to check that pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate for 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we can see that for any c∈Cc\in C,

𝐄𝒟𝒳[c⁡(𝐱)​(p∗​(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})(p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x}))] =12​𝐄𝒟𝒳[c⁡(𝐱)​g^​(𝐱)]≤τ.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})\widehat{g}(\mathbf{x})]\leq\tau.

The latter inequality follows from the condition on gg in the statement of the theorem.

Similary, we can check that,

𝐄𝒟𝒳[c⁡(𝐱)​(p∗​(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})(p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x}))] =12​𝐄𝒟𝒳[c⁡(𝐱)​g^​(𝐱)]≥−τ.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})\widehat{g}(\mathbf{x})]\geq-\tau.

Thus, pp is (C,τ)(C,\tau)-multiaccurate.
