We observe that p⁡(x)∈{0,12,1}p(x)\in\left\{0,\frac{1}{2},1\right\}. For any such vv in the range of pp, as we have picked f∈Cf\in C, the condition on gg in the theorem statement shows that |cor⁡(𝐲,p⁡(𝐱)|p⁡(𝐱)=v)|≤τ|\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},p(\mathbf{x})|p(\mathbf{x})=v)|\leq\tau.

On the other hand, we can also observe that (using Eqn. (6)),

cor⁡(𝐲,f)\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},f) =𝐄[(2​𝐲−1)​f​(𝐱)]\displaystyle=\E[(2\mathbf{y}-1)f(\mathbf{x})]
=𝐄[(2​p∗​(𝐱)−1)​f​(𝐱)]\displaystyle=\E[(2p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-1)f(\mathbf{x})]
=12𝐄[(f^(𝐱)+g^(𝐱))f(𝐱)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\E[(\widehat{f}(\mathbf{x})+\widehat{g}(\mathbf{x}))f(\mathbf{x})]
≥q−τ.\displaystyle\geq q-\tau.

Thus as long as q>τq>\tau, there is a function in 𝒞\mathcal{C} with non-trivial correlation with 𝐲\mathbf{y}, but no post-processing of pp yields a weak agnostic learner with correlation better than τ\tau. (Note that if qq is almost 00 for every f∈𝒞f\in\mathcal{C}, then 𝒞\mathcal{C} only contains almost constant (w.r.t 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}) functions.) ∎

Remark 4.3.

The existence of a gg satisfying the conditions in the statement of Theorem 4.2 with τ\tau being negligible follows from the existence of one-way functions as long as 𝒞\mathcal{C} is contained in the class of polynomial-sized circuits [15]. We have assumed above that pp can be a randomized predictor; again this assumption can be removed assuming the existence of one-way functions. Also note that if every c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} is balanced, then we get q=1/2q=1/2; this was the case with the class used in Theorem 4.1.

The following theorem shows that Theorem 4.1 is tight in the sense that whenever the optimal correlation is noticeably greater than 1/21/2, then a simple transformation p↦2​p−1p\mapsto 2p-1, does indeed provide a weak agnostic learning guarantee.

Theorem 4.4.

For any 𝒞,𝒟\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}, one can post-process a (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate predictor to obtain a (α,2​α−1−2​τ)(\alpha,2\alpha-1-2\tau)-weak agnostic learning for 𝒞\mathcal{C} under the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}. In particular, any (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate predictor pp for 𝒟\mathcal{D} satisfies

cor𝒟​(𝐲,2​p​(𝐱)−1)≥2​maxc∈𝒞​cor𝒟​(𝐲,c⁡(𝐱))−1−2​τ.\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},2p(\mathbf{x})-1)\geq 2\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))-1-2\tau.
Proof.

Let pp be a (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate predictor with respect to 𝒟\mathcal{D}. We have the following for any c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}.

cor𝒟​(𝐲,c)\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c) =cor𝒟​(p∗,c)\displaystyle=\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(p^{*},c)
=𝐄𝒟[(2​p∗​(𝐱)−1)​c​(𝐱)]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}}[(2p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-1)c(\mathbf{x})]
=𝐄𝒟[c⁡(𝐱)​(p∗​(𝐱)−(1−p∗​(𝐱)))​(p⁡(𝐱)+(1−p⁡(𝐱)))]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}}[c(\mathbf{x})(p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-(1-p^{*}(\mathbf{x})))(p(\mathbf{x})+(1-p(\mathbf{x})))]
=𝐄𝒟[c(𝐱)(p∗(𝐱)p(𝐱)−(1−p∗(𝐱))(1−p(𝐱))]+𝐄𝒟[c(𝐱)(p∗(𝐱)−p(𝐱))]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}}[c(\mathbf{x})(p^{*}(\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})-(1-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))(1-p(\mathbf{x}))]+\E_{\mathcal{D}}[c(\mathbf{x})(p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x}))]
≤𝐄𝒟[|c⁡(𝐱)|​|p∗​(𝐱)​p​(𝐱)−(1−p∗​(𝐱))​(1−p⁡(𝐱))|]+τ\displaystyle\leq\E_{\mathcal{D}}[|c(\mathbf{x})||p^{*}(\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})-(1-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))(1-p(\mathbf{x}))|]+\tau
≤𝐄𝒟[p∗​(𝐱)​p​(𝐱)+(1−p∗​(𝐱))​(1−p⁡(𝐱))]+τ.\displaystyle\leq\E_{\mathcal{D}}[p^{*}(\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})+(1-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))(1-p(\mathbf{x}))]+\tau.

Above, in the penultimate inequality, we used the fact that pp satisfies (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccuracy with respect to 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and in the final inequality, we use the fact that |c⁡(𝐱)|≤1|c(\mathbf{x})|\leq 1, and that

|p∗​(𝐱)​p​(𝐱)−(1−p∗​(𝐱))​(1−p⁡(𝐱))|≤p∗​(𝐱)​p​(𝐱)+(1−p∗​(𝐱))​(1−p⁡(𝐱)),|p^{*}(\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})-(1-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))(1-p(\mathbf{x}))|\leq p^{*}(\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})+(1-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))(1-p(\mathbf{x})),

since both p⁡(𝐱),p∗​(𝐱)∈[0,1]p(\mathbf{x}),p^{*}(\mathbf{x})\in[0,1].

On the other hand, one can easily check the following identity for a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}:

(2​a−1)​(2​b−1)=2​(a​b+(1−a)​(1−b))−1.(2a-1)(2b-1)=2(ab+(1-a)(1-b))-1.

Using this we write

cor𝒟​(𝐲,2​p−1)\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},2p-1) =cor𝒟​(p∗,2​p−1)\displaystyle=\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(p^{*},2p-1)
=𝐄𝒟[(2​p∗​(𝐱)−1)​(2​p​(𝐱)−1)]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}}[(2p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-1)(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)]
=2​𝐄𝒟[p∗​(𝐱)​p​(𝐱)+(1−p∗​(𝐱))​(1−p⁡(𝐱))]−1.\displaystyle=2\E_{\mathcal{D}}[p^{*}(\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})+(1-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))(1-p(\mathbf{x}))]-1.

Combining the two inequalities, we get that,

cor𝒟​(𝐲,2​p−1)\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},2p-1) ≥2​maxc∈𝒞​cor𝒟​(𝐲,c)−1−2​τ,\displaystyle\geq 2\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c)-1-2\tau,

which proves the claim. ∎

4.2 Strong Agnostic Learning from Calibrated Multiaccuracy

In this section, we show that provided the predictor pp that is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate is also well-calibrated, then sign⁡(2​p−1)\mathrm{sign}(2p-1) in fact is a strong agnostic learner. Interestingly, our proof decomposes the roles of multiaccuracy and calibration neatly and highlights the contribution that both these properties make in order to obtain a strong agnostic learning guarantee. We will assume in this section that the hypothesis class CC contains functions from 𝒳→[−1,1]\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1]; as discussed in Section 3.2, this is essentially without loss of any generality.

Assume that pp is well-calibrated. It is intuitive that pp should do much better than random guessing, since when it predicts v∈[0,1]v\in[0,1], the expected value of the label is indeed vv. The only exception to this is if the predictor always predicts values vv close to 1/21/2. We can formalize this as follows:

Lemma 4.5.

Let pp be τ\tau-calibrated for some distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} over 𝒳×{0,1}\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\}. Then

cor𝒟(𝐲,sign(2p(𝐱)−1))≥2𝐄[|p(𝐱)−12|]−2τ.\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},\mathrm{sign}(2p(\mathbf{x})-1))\geq 2\E\left[\left|p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right|\right]-2\tau.
Proof.

We can write

cor𝒟​(𝐲,sign⁡(2​p​(𝐱)−1))\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},\mathrm{sign}(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)) =𝐄𝒟[sign⁡(2​p​(𝐱)−1)​(2​𝐲−1)]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{sign}(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)(2\mathbf{y}-1)]
=𝐄𝒟[sign(2p(𝐱)−1)(2𝐄[𝐲|p(𝐱)]−1)]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{sign}(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)(2\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]-1)]
=𝐄𝒟[sign⁡(2​p​(𝐱)−1)​(2​p​(𝐱)−1)]+2​𝐄𝒟[sign⁡(2​p​(x)−1)​(𝐄[𝐲|p⁡(𝐱)]−p⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{sign}(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)]+2\E_{\mathcal{D}}[\mathrm{sign}(2p(x)-1)(\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]-p(\mathbf{x}))]
≥𝐄𝒟[|2p(𝐱)−1|]−2𝐄[|𝐄[𝐲|p(𝐱)]−p(𝐱)|]\displaystyle\geq\E_{\mathcal{D}}[|2p(\mathbf{x})-1|]-2\E[|\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]-p(\mathbf{x})|]
≥2​𝐄𝒟[|p⁡(𝐱)−12|]−2​τ.\displaystyle\geq 2\E_{\mathcal{D}}\left[\left|p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right|\right]-2\tau.

The last inequality follows from the definition of τ\tau-calibration. ∎

Next we show that if 𝒞\mathcal{C} contains a hypothesis that correlates well with the labels, and if pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate, then pp cannot always predict values close to 1/21/2.

Lemma 4.6.

If pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate for the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, then for every c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C},

𝐄𝒟[|p⁡(𝐱)−12|]≥cor𝒟​(𝐲,c​(𝐱))2−τ.\E_{\mathcal{D}}\left[\left|p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right|\right]\geq\frac{\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))}{2}-\tau.
Proof.

Fix any c∈Cc\in C. Since pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate, we have

𝐄𝒟[c⁡(𝐱)​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle\E_{\mathcal{D}}[c(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))] ≤τ.\displaystyle\leq\tau. (7)
We can also write
𝐄𝒟[c⁡(𝐱)​(𝐲−12)]\displaystyle\E_{\mathcal{D}}\left[c(\mathbf{x})\left(\mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right] =cor𝒟​(𝐲,c​(𝐱))2.\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))}{2}. (8)
Subtracting Equation (7) from (8) gives
𝐄𝒟[c⁡(𝐱)​(p⁡(𝐱)−12)]\displaystyle\E_{\mathcal{D}}\left[c(\mathbf{x})\left(p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right] ≥cor𝒟​(𝐲,c​(𝐱))2−τ.\displaystyle\geq\frac{\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))}{2}-\tau.

The claim now follows by Hölder’s inequality, since

𝐄𝒟[c⁡(𝐱)​(p⁡(𝐱)−12)]\displaystyle\E_{\mathcal{D}}\left[c(\mathbf{x})\left(p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right] ≤max𝐱|c⁡(𝐱)|𝐄[|p⁡(𝐱)−12|]≤𝐄[|p⁡(𝐱)−12|],\displaystyle\leq\max_{\mathbf{x}}|c(\mathbf{x})|\E\left[\left|p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right|\right]\leq\E\left[\left|p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right|\right],

given that |c⁡(𝐱)|≤1|c(\mathbf{x})|\leq 1 for all c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}. ∎

The proof of Theorem 4.7 below follows immediately from Lemmas 4.5 (which applies to τ\tau-calibrated predictors) and 4.6 (which applies to (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate predictors). This shows provided that for any τ>0\tau>0 it is possible to construct a predictor pp that is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate for 𝒟\mathcal{D} such that pp is also τ\tau-calibrated, then sign⁡(2​p−1)\mathrm{sign}(2p-1) yields a strong agnostic learning guarantee for the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} under 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

Theorem 4.7.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a hypothesis class and τ>0\tau>0. Suppose pp is a predictor that is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate and τ\tau-calibrated with respect to 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Then, sign⁡(2​p−1)\mathrm{sign}(2p-1) satisfies,

cor(𝐲,sign(2p(𝐱)−1))]≥maxc∈𝒞cor(𝐲,c(𝐱))−4τ.\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},\mathrm{sign}(2p(\mathbf{x})-1))]\geq\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))-4\tau.
Proof.
cor⁡(𝐲,sign⁡(2​p​(𝐱)−1))\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},\mathrm{sign}(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)) ≥2𝐄[|p(𝐱)−12|]−2τ\displaystyle\geq 2\E\left[\left|p(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2}\right|\right]-2\tau pp is τ\tau-calibrated (Lemma 4.5)
≥2⋅(cor𝒟​(𝐲,c​(𝐱))2−τ)−2​τ\displaystyle\geq 2\cdot\Bigg(\frac{\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))}{2}-\tau\Bigg)-2\tau pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate (Lemma 4.6)
≥cor𝒟​(𝐲,c⁡(𝐱))−4​τ.\displaystyle\geq\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},c(\mathbf{x}))-4\tau.

∎

5 Hardcore Measures with Optimal Density

In this section we consider a domain 𝒳\mathcal{X} endowed with a base distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}. We encourage the reader to think of 𝒳={0,1}n\mathcal{X}=\{0,1\}^{n} and 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} to be the uniform distribution. A measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a function μ:𝒳→[0,1]\mu:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1], which is not identically 00. A measure μ\mu defines a probability distribution μ¯\bar{\mu} by setting

μ¯​(𝐱)=Pr𝒟𝒳[𝐱=x]μ(𝐱)𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[μ⁡(𝐱)].\bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mathbf{x}=x]\mu(\mathbf{x})}{\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu(\mathbf{x})]}.

Given a measure μ:𝒳→[0,1]\mu:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1] and a base distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the density of μ\mu in 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} is given by

𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)=𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[μ⁡(𝐱)].\mathsf{dns}(\mu)=\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu(\mathbf{x})].

We drop 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} from the density notation, but note that this is density with respect to the base distribution. Density measures the min-entropy of a distribution since

maxx∈𝒳⁡μ¯​(x)Pr𝒟𝒳[𝐱=x]=maxx∈𝒳⁡μ⁡(x)𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[μ⁡(𝐱)]=maxx⁡μ⁡(x)𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)≤1𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)\displaystyle\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{\bar{\mu}(x)}{\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mathbf{x}=x]}=\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\frac{\mu(x)}{\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu(\mathbf{x})]}=\frac{\max_{x}\mu(x)}{\mathsf{dns}(\mu)}\leq\frac{1}{\mathsf{dns}(\mu)} (9)

When considering hardcore measures, we will restrict 𝒞={c:𝒳→{0,1}}\mathcal{C}=\{c:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}\} to be a class of Boolean functions, rather than bounded functions. We will assume that it contains the constant functions 0,1\mathrm{0},\mathrm{1} and is closed under complement. In complexity theory, given a class of distinguisher functions 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we are interested in studying how well the functions c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} can approximate the outputs of a given boolean function gg. We quantify the hardness of gg with respect to a class of functions 𝒞\mathcal{C} and a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} on 𝒳\mathcal{X} as follows:

Definition 5.1 (Hardness of a function).

Given a class 𝒞={c:𝒳→{0,1}}\mathcal{C}=\{c:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\}\}, a function g:𝒳→{0,1}g:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\}, a distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and δ>0\delta>0, we say that gg is (𝒞,δ)(\mathcal{C},\delta)-hard on 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} if for all c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C},

Pr𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[c(𝐱)=g(𝐱)]≤1−δ.\Pr_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})=g(\mathbf{x})]\leq 1-\delta.

We say a distribution is hardcore when δ\delta becomes arbitrarily close to 1/21/2, since this means that it is hard to predict the values of gg much better than random guessing. A hardcore measure μ\mu is one which induces a hardcore distribution μ¯\bar{\mu}.

Definition 5.2 (Relative complexity of a function and a function class [29, Definition 6]).

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a family of functions f:𝒳→[0,1]f\colon\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1]. A function hh has complexity (t,q)(t,q) relative to 𝒞\mathcal{C} if it can be computed by an oracle-aided circuit of size tt with qq oracle gates, where each oracle gate is instantiated with a function from 𝒞\mathcal{C}. We denote by 𝒞t,q\mathcal{C}_{t,q} the class of functions that have complexity at most (t,q)(t,q) relative to 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Impagliazzo’s hardcore lemma [28] studies boolean functions gg that are somewhat hard to predict, and it shows that for these functions we can always find a hardcore measure μ\mu (called a hardcore measure) such that, under the distribution μ¯\bar{\mu}, the function gg is very hard to compute with respect to 𝒞\mathcal{C}, one cannot improve much over random guessing. Formally:

Theorem 5.3 (IHCL, [28, 25]).

Let 𝒞={c:𝒳→{0,1}}\mathcal{C}=\{c:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\}\} be a family of functions, let 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} be a probability distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and let ϵ,δ>0\epsilon,\delta>0. There exist t=poly⁡(log⁡|𝒳|,1/ϵ,1/δ)t=\mathrm{poly}(\log|\mathcal{X}|,1/\epsilon,1/\delta) and q=​p​o​l​y​(1/ϵ,1/δ)q=\emph{poly}(1/\epsilon,1/\delta) such that the following holds: If g:𝒳→{0,1}g:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\} is (𝒞t,q,δ)(\mathcal{C}_{t,q},\delta)-hard on 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, then there is a measure μ\mu satisfying:

  • •

    Hardness: gg is (𝒞,1/2−ϵ)(\mathcal{C},1/2-\epsilon)-hard on μ¯\bar{\mu}.

  • •

    Optimal density: 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)=2​δ\mathsf{dns}(\mu)=2\delta.

Impagliazzo’s original proof gives density δ\delta [28], the improvement to the optimal 2​δ2\delta is due to Holenstein [25].

We now define the set of balanced under calibration measures, which play a key role in our result.

Definition 5.4.

Define the weight function w𝖬𝖺𝗑:[0,1]→[1,2]w_{\mathsf{Max}}:[0,1]\to[1,2] as w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p)=1/max⁡(p,1−p)w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p)=1/\max(p,1-p) and the weight function family

W={w:[0,1]→[1,2]s.t.w(p)∈[1,w𝖬𝖺𝗑(p)]}.W=\{w:[0,1]\to[1,2]\ s.t.\ w(p)\in[1,w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p)]\}.

Given g:𝒳→{0,1}g:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} and p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1], we define the set M⁡(p,g)M(p,g) of balanced under calibration measures to be {μw}w∈W\{\mu_{w}\}_{w\in W} where

μw​(x)=w⁡(p⁡(x))⋅|g⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|​for​w∈W.\mu_{w}(x)=w(p(x))\cdot|g(x)-p(x)|\ \text{for}\ w\in W.

We define the the maximal balanced under calibration measure μ𝖬𝖺𝗑∈M⁡(p,g)\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}\in M(p,g) as

μ𝖬𝖺𝗑​(x)=w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p⁡(x))⋅|g⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}(x)=w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p(x))\cdot|g(x)-p(x)|

while the minimal balanced under calibration measure is μ𝖳𝖳𝖵​(x)=|g⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}}(x)=|g(x)-p(x)|, corresponding to w=1w=1.

The condition μ⁡(x)∈[0,1]\mu(x)\in[0,1] requires the constraint w⁡(p⁡(x))≤w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p⁡(x))≤2w(p(x))\leq w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p(x))\leq 2. We also impose the condition w⁡(p)≥1w(p)\geq 1 since the goal is to find large/dense measures, so there is no point in choosing weights less than 11. Intuitively, this ensures that, across the level sets SvS_{v}, the measure μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} assigns higher probability measure to level sets with vv value closer to 1/21/2, which increases the hardness of gg when sampling according to the measure. We note following chain of inequalities:

μ𝖳𝖳𝖵​(x)≤μ⁡(x)≤μ𝖬𝖺𝗑​(x)≤2​μ𝖳𝖳𝖵​(x).\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}}(x)\leq\mu(x)\leq\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}(x)\leq 2\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}}(x).

Some comments on the density and hardness of distributions in M⁡(p,g)M(p,g):

  • •

    As wμw_{\mu} increases from 11 to w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p)w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p), μ⁡(x)\mu(x) and hence 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)=𝐄𝒟𝒳[μ⁡(𝐱)]\mathsf{dns}(\mu)=\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu(\mathbf{x})] increases. However, it is less clear how the hardness of the distribution μ¯\bar{\mu} changes, since this changes the balance of weight between the different level sets. Indeed, as we shall see, all these distributions are hard, under suitable assumptions on pp (pp being multicalibrated will suffice).

  • •

    In contrast with μ𝖳𝖳𝖵\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}}, μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} gives (nearly) twice as much weight to the level sets where p⁡(x)≈1/2p(x)\approx 1/2, which intuitively is the region where gg is hardest for the predictors in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. So one might hope that (under suitable assumptions about the predictor pp) μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} is indeed hardcore, and has density 2​δ2\delta.

  • •

    For pp close to {0,1}\{0,1\}, w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p)≈1w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p)\approx 1 and μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} and μ𝖳𝖳𝖵\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}} are almost equal. For distributions where pp takes such values with reasonable probability, if μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} is indeed 2​δ2\delta dense, it suggests that the density of μ𝖳𝖳𝖵\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}} is in fact greater than δ\delta.

5.1 Weighted Multiaccuracy and Hardcore Measures

We define the notion of weighted multiaccuracy, which applies to distributions on 𝒳×{0,1}\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\}.

Definition 5.5 (Weighted multiaccuracy).

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be a distribution on 𝒳×{0,1}\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\}, let 𝒞={c:𝒳→{0,1}}\mathcal{C}=\{c:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\}\} be a class of functions, let p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1] be predictor, and w:[0,1]→ℝ+w:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+} a weight function. We define the (w,𝒞)(w,\mathcal{C})-multiaccuracy error of pp under the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} as

𝖬𝖠𝒟​(w,𝒞,p)=maxc∈𝒞⁡|𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[c⁡(𝐱)​w​(p⁡(𝐱))​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))]|.\mathsf{MA}_{\mathcal{D}}(w,\mathcal{C},p)=\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\Big|\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[c(\mathbf{x})w(p(\mathbf{x}))(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))]\Big|.

We say that the predictor pp is (w,𝒞,ε)(w,\mathcal{C},\varepsilon)-multiaccurate for 𝒟\mathcal{D} if 𝖬𝖠𝒟​(w,𝒞,p)≤ϵ\mathsf{MA}_{\mathcal{D}}(w,\mathcal{C},p)\leq\epsilon.

Given a distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} on 𝒳\mathcal{X} and g:𝒳→{0,1}g:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}, define the distribution 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g} on (𝐱,𝐲)∈𝒳×{0,1}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\in\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\} where 𝐱∼𝒟𝒳\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} and 𝐲=g⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{y}=g(\mathbf{x}). We relate the hardness of predicting gg using functions from 𝒞\mathcal{C} under μ¯w\bar{\mu}_{w} to the ww-weighted multiaccuracy error of pp for the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} under distribution 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g}.

Lemma 5.6.

If 𝖬𝖠𝒟g​(w,𝒞,p)≤ε\mathsf{MA}_{\mathcal{D}^{g}}(w,\mathcal{C},p)\leq\varepsilon, then gg is (1/2−3​ε/(2​𝖽𝗇𝗌​(μw)))\big(1/2-3\varepsilon/(2\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{w}))\big)-hard for 𝒞\mathcal{C} under μ¯w\bar{\mu}_{w}.

Before we prove Lemma 5.6, we show some intermediate results. Let μ¯\bar{\mu} denote a distribution on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Let η=𝐄μ¯[g⁡(x)]\eta=\E_{\bar{\mu}}[g(x)]. The function class 𝒞\mathcal{C} can trivially approximate gg to accuracy max⁡(η,1−η)\max(\eta,1-\eta) under the distribution μ¯\bar{\mu} by using a constant function. To characterize how much better 𝒞\mathcal{C} can do, we define

corμ¯​(g,𝒞)=maxc∈𝒞⁡|corμ¯​(g,c)|=maxc∈𝒞⁡|𝐄𝐱∼μ¯[(2​g​(𝐱)−1)​c​(𝐱)]|.\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}}(g,\mathcal{C})=\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}|\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}}(g,c)|=\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\left|\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\bar{\mu}}[(2g(\mathbf{x})-1)c(\mathbf{x})]\right|.

The next lemma shows that this captures the hardness of gg for the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, under the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

Lemma 5.7.

We have

min(η,1−η)+corμ¯(g,𝒞)≤maxc∈𝒞Pr𝐱∼μ¯[c(𝐱)=g(𝐱)]≤max(η,1−η)+corμ¯(g,𝒞).\displaystyle\min(\eta,1-\eta)+\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}}(g,\mathcal{C})\leq\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\Pr_{\mathbf{x}\sim\bar{\mu}}[c(\mathbf{x})=g(\mathbf{x})]\leq\max(\eta,1-\eta)+\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}}(g,\mathcal{C}). (10)
Proof.

We can write

Prμ¯[c(𝐱)=g(𝐱)]\displaystyle\Pr_{\bar{\mu}}[c(\mathbf{x})=g(\mathbf{x})] =𝐄μ¯[12​(1+(2​c​(𝐱)−1)​(2​g​(𝐱)−1))]\displaystyle=\E_{\bar{\mu}}\left[\frac{1}{2}(1+(2c(\mathbf{x})-1)(2g(\mathbf{x})-1))\right]
=𝐄μ¯[c⁡(𝐱)​(2​g​(𝐱)−1)+(1−g⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle=\E_{\bar{\mu}}[c(\mathbf{x})(2g(\mathbf{x})-1)+(1-g(\mathbf{x}))]
=corμ¯​(g,c)+1−η.\displaystyle=\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}}(g,c)+1-\eta.
Recall that c¯=1−c\bar{c}=1-c and that we are assuming that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is closed under complementation. So we have
Prμ¯[c¯(𝐱)=g(𝐱)]\displaystyle\Pr_{\bar{\mu}}[\bar{c}(\mathbf{x})=g(\mathbf{x})] =1−Prμ¯[c(𝐱)=g(𝐱)]\displaystyle=1-\Pr_{\bar{\mu}}[c(\mathbf{x})=g(\mathbf{x})]
=𝐄μ¯[g(𝐱)]−𝐄μ¯[c(𝐱)(2g(𝐱)−1)]]\displaystyle=\E_{\bar{\mu}}[g(\mathbf{x})]-\E_{\bar{\mu}}[c(\mathbf{x})(2g(\mathbf{x})-1)]]
=η−corμ¯​(g,c).\displaystyle=\eta-\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}}(g,c).

The upper bound of max⁡(η,1−η)+|corμ¯​(g,c)|\max(\eta,1-\eta)+|\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}}(g,c)| holds in both cases. The upper bound follows by maximizing over all c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}.

To prove the lower bound, in order to predict gg with accuracy min⁡(η,1−η)+|corμ¯​(g,c)|\min(\eta,1-\eta)+|\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}}(g,c)|, we use cc if corμ¯​(g,c)≥0\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}}(g,c)\geq 0; else we use c¯\bar{c}, which also lies in 𝒞\mathcal{C} by assumption. Maximizing over c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} gives the claimed bound. ∎

Equation (10) gives tight bounds on the prediction advantage of 𝒞\mathcal{C} for balanced functions where η≈1/2\eta\approx 1/2. In general, it characterizes the advantage to within an additive |1−2​η||1-2\eta|, since

max⁡(η,1−η)−min⁡(η,1−η)=|1−2​η|.\max(\eta,1-\eta)-\min(\eta,1-\eta)=|1-2\eta|.

Lemma 5.7 can be seen as a generalization of Yao’s Lemma relating unpredictability with indistinguishability (see Lemma 2.14 in [8] for a formal statement).

For balanced under calibration measures, we can relate correlation of 𝒞\mathcal{C} with gg under the distribution μ¯w\bar{\mu}_{w} to the (w,𝒞)(w,\mathcal{C})-weighted multiaccuracy error for the labeled distribution 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g} on (𝐱,𝐲)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) where 𝐱∼𝒟\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D} and 𝐲=g⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{y}=g(\mathbf{x}).

Lemma 5.8.

Consider a distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, a labeling function g:𝒳→{0,1}g:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}, a predictor pp, a weight function w∈Ww\in W and the corresponding measure μw∈M⁡(p,g)\mu_{w}\in M(p,g). Then

𝖬𝖠𝒟g​(w,𝒞,p)=corμ¯w​(𝒞,g)⋅𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μw).\mathsf{MA}_{\mathcal{D}^{g}}(w,\mathcal{C},p)=\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}_{w}}(\mathcal{C},g)\cdot\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{w}).

For y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] we have the identity |y−t|⋅(2​y−1)=y−t|y-t|\cdot(2y-1)=y-t. Applying this with 𝐲=g⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{y}=g(\mathbf{x}) and t=p⁡(𝐱)t=p(\mathbf{x}), we can write

𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟g[c⁡(𝐱)​w​(p⁡(𝐱))​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}^{g}}[c(\mathbf{x})w(p(\mathbf{x}))(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))] =𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[c⁡(𝐱)​w​(p⁡(𝐱))​(g⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})w(p(\mathbf{x}))(g(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x}))]
=𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[c⁡(𝐱)​w​(p⁡(𝐱))⋅|g⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱)|⋅(2​g​(𝐱)−1)]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[c(\mathbf{x})w(p(\mathbf{x}))\cdot|g(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x})|\cdot(2g(\mathbf{x})-1)]
=𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[μw​(𝐱)​c​(𝐱)​(2​g​(𝐱)−1)]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu_{w}(\mathbf{x})c(\mathbf{x})(2g(\mathbf{x})-1)]
=𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[μw​(𝐱)​c​(𝐱)​(2​g​(𝐱)−1)]𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[μw​(𝐱)]⋅𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[μw​(𝐱)]\displaystyle=\frac{\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu_{w}(\mathbf{x})c(\mathbf{x})(2g(\mathbf{x})-1)]}{\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu_{w}(\mathbf{x})]}\cdot\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu_{w}(\mathbf{x})]

Two steps above, we used the fact that μw​(𝐱)=w⁡(p⁡(𝐱))⋅|g⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱)|\mu_{w}(\mathbf{x})=w(p(\mathbf{x}))\cdot|g(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x})|. Taking the absolute value on either side and maximizing over all c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} gives the claimed result. ∎

We use this to prove that weighted multiaccuracy of pp under 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g} implies gg is hard for 𝒞\mathcal{C} under μ¯w\bar{\mu}_{w}.

Proof of Lemma 5.6.

maxc∈𝒞Pr𝐱∼μ¯w[c(𝐱)=g(𝐱)]\displaystyle\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\Pr_{\mathbf{x}\sim\bar{\mu}_{w}}[c(\mathbf{x})=g(\mathbf{x})] ≤max⁡(η,1−η)+corμ¯w​(𝒞,g)\displaystyle\leq\max(\eta,1-\eta)+\mathrm{cor}_{\bar{\mu}_{w}}(\mathcal{C},g)

5.2 Optimal Density Analysis Using Calibration

[46] showed a lower bound on the density of μ𝖳𝖳𝖵\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}} assuming that gg that gg is δ\delta-hard for 𝒞t,q\mathcal{C}_{t,q}, which is expressive enough to compute 𝟏[p(x)≥ψ]\mathbf{1}[p(x)\geq\psi] for ψ∈[0,1]\psi\in[0,1]. Since μ𝖳𝖳𝖵\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}} is the minimal measure in M⁡(p,g)M(p,g), this implies the same lower bound for every measure in M⁡(p,g)M(p,g). We recall their argument below.

Lemma 5.9 ([46]).

Assuming gg is δ\delta-hard for 𝒞t,q\mathcal{C}_{t,q} under distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, for every μ∈M⁡(p,g)\mu\in M(p,g), we have 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)≥δ\mathsf{dns}(\mu)\geq\delta.

Proof.

We have 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ𝖳𝖳𝖵)=𝐄[|g⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱)|]\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}})=\E[|g(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x})|]. But |g⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱)||g(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x})| is the error probability of the randomized function which outputs 11 with probability p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}). By averaging, there exists a deterministic threshold ψ∈[0,1]\psi\in[0,1] so that the deterministic function p~(x)=𝟏[p(x)≥ψ]\tilde{p}(x)=\mathbf{1}[p(x)\geq\psi] does as well. But since p~∈𝒞t,q\tilde{p}\in\mathcal{C}_{t,q}, this implies that 𝖽𝗇𝗌𝒟​(μ𝖳𝖳𝖵)≥δ\mathsf{dns}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}})\geq\delta.

Every μ∈M⁡(p,g)\mu\in M(p,g) satisfies 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)≥𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ𝖳𝖳𝖵)\mathsf{dns}(\mu)\geq\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}}), so the claim follows. ∎

Note that the analysis above uses very little about the predictor, other than an upper bound on its complexity. We will prove a stronger bound under the additional assumption that pp is a calibrated predictor for gg under 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g}. This part of the argument will not rely on multiaccuracy, weighted or otherwise.

Lemma 5.10.

Assume that the predictor pp is τ\tau-calibrated for 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g}. Then we have

|𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μw)−2​𝐄𝒟𝒳[w⁡(p⁡(𝐱))​p​(𝐱)​(1−p⁡(𝐱))]|≤2​τ.\left|\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{w})-2\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[w(p(\mathbf{x}))p(\mathbf{x})(1-p(\mathbf{x}))]\right|\leq 2\tau.
Proof.

We will use the following identity for v∈[0,1]v\in[0,1] and y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} which can be viewed as the multilinear expansion of |y−v||y-v|:

|y−v|=y⁡(1−2​v)+v.|y-v|=y(1-2v)+v.

Using this with y=g⁡(x)y=g(x) and v=p⁡(x)v=p(x) we can write

𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μw)\displaystyle\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{w}) =𝐄𝒟𝒳[μw​(𝐱)]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mu_{w}(\mathbf{x})]
=𝐄𝒟𝒳[w⁡(p⁡(𝐱))⋅|g⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱)|]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[w(p(\mathbf{x}))\cdot|g(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x})|]
=𝐄𝒟𝒳[w⁡(p⁡(𝐱))​(g⁡(𝐱)​(1−2​p​(𝐱))+p⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[w(p(\mathbf{x}))(g(\mathbf{x})(1-2p(\mathbf{x}))+p(\mathbf{x}))]
=𝐄𝒟𝒳[w⁡(p⁡(𝐱))​(p⁡(𝐱)​(1−2​p​(𝐱))+p⁡(𝐱))]+𝐄𝒟𝒳[w⁡(p⁡(𝐱))​(1−2​p​(𝐱))​(g⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[w(p(\mathbf{x}))(p(\mathbf{x})(1-2p(\mathbf{x}))+p(\mathbf{x}))]+\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[w(p(\mathbf{x}))(1-2p(\mathbf{x}))(g(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x}))]

Hence we have

|𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μw)−2​𝐄𝒟𝒳[w⁡(p⁡(𝐱))​p​(𝐱)​(1−p⁡(𝐱))]|=|𝐄𝒟𝒳[w⁡(p⁡(𝐱))​(1−2​p​(𝐱))​(g⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱))]|.\displaystyle\left|\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{w})-2\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[w(p(\mathbf{x}))p(\mathbf{x})(1-p(\mathbf{x}))]\right|=\left|\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[w(p(\mathbf{x}))(1-2p(\mathbf{x}))(g(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x}))]\right|. (12)

Since w⁡(p)∈[1,2]w(p)\in[1,2] and 1−2​p∈[−1,1]1-2p\in[-1,1], we have |w⁡(p)​(1−2​p)|≤2|w(p)(1-2p)|\leq 2. Since pp is τ\tau-calibrated, by Equation (4) applied to v⁡(p)=w⁡(p)​(1−2​p)/2v(p)=w(p)(1-2p)/2, the predictor pp satisfies the bound

|𝐄𝒟𝒳[w⁡(p⁡(𝐱))​(1−2​p​(𝐱))​(g⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱))]|≤2​τ.\displaystyle\left|\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[w(p(\mathbf{x}))(1-2p(\mathbf{x}))(g(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x}))]\right|\leq 2\tau.

Plugging this into Equation (12) gives the claimed bound. ∎

Lemma 5.11.

Assume that gg is δ\delta-hard for 𝒞t,q\mathcal{C}_{t,q} under 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, and pp is τ\tau-calibrated for 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g}. Then

𝐄𝒟𝒳[min⁡(p⁡(𝐱),1−p⁡(𝐱))]≥δ−τ.\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\min(p(\mathbf{x}),1-p(\mathbf{x}))]\geq\delta-\tau.
Proof.

Consider the function f(x)=𝟏[p(x)≥1/2]f(x)=\mathbf{1}[p(x)\geq 1/2]. This function is computable in 𝒞t,q\mathcal{C}_{t,q}. The function ff errs when g⁡(x)=1g(x)=1 for points where p⁡(x)<1/2p(x)<1/2 and whenever g⁡(x)=0g(x)=0 otherwise. So we can write

δ\displaystyle\delta ≤Pr𝒟𝒳[f(𝐱)≠g(𝐱)]\displaystyle\leq\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[f(\mathbf{x})\neq g(\mathbf{x})]
=Pr𝒟𝒳[g(𝐱)=1∧p(𝐱)<1/2]+Pr𝒟𝒳[g(𝐱)=0∧p(𝐱)≥1/2]\displaystyle=\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[g(\mathbf{x})=1\wedge p(\mathbf{x})<1/2]+\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[g(\mathbf{x})=0\wedge p(\mathbf{x})\geq 1/2]
=𝐄𝒟g[𝐄[𝐲|p(𝐱)]⋅𝟏[p(𝐱)<1/2]+(1−𝐄[𝐲|p(𝐱)])⋅𝟏[p(𝐱)≥1/2]]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}^{g}}[\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]\cdot\mathbf{1}[p(\mathbf{x})<1/2]+(1-\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})])\cdot\mathbf{1}[p(\mathbf{x})\geq 1/2]]
=𝐄𝒟g[(p(𝐱)+𝐄[𝐲|p(𝐱)]−p(𝐱))⋅𝟏[p(𝐱)<1/2]+(1−p(𝐱)+p(𝐱)−𝐄𝒟g[𝐲|p(𝐱)])⋅𝟏[p(𝐱)≥1/2]]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}^{g}}[(p(\mathbf{x})+\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]-p(\mathbf{x}))\cdot\mathbf{1}[p(\mathbf{x})<1/2]+(1-p(\mathbf{x})+p(\mathbf{x})-\E_{\mathcal{D}^{g}}[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})])\cdot\mathbf{1}[p(\mathbf{x})\geq 1/2]]
≤𝐄𝒟g[(p(𝐱)⋅𝟏[p(𝐱)<1/2]+(1−p(𝐱))⋅𝟏[p(𝐱)≥1/2])]+𝐄𝒟g[|p(𝐱)−𝐄[𝐲|p(𝐱)]|]\displaystyle\leq\E_{\mathcal{D}^{g}}[(p(\mathbf{x})\cdot\mathbf{1}[p(\mathbf{x})<1/2]+(1-p(\mathbf{x}))\cdot\mathbf{1}[p(\mathbf{x})\geq 1/2])]+\E_{\mathcal{D}^{g}}[|p(\mathbf{x})-\E[\mathbf{y}|p(\mathbf{x})]|]
=𝐄𝒟𝒳[min(p(𝐱),1−p(𝐱)]+𝖤𝖢𝖤(p,𝒟g),\displaystyle=\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\min(p(\mathbf{x}),1-p(\mathbf{x})]+\mathsf{ECE}(p,\mathcal{D}^{g}),

where we use the identity that

min(v,1−v)=v⋅𝟏[v<1/2]+(1−v)⋅𝟏[v≥1/2].\min(v,1-v)=v\cdot\mathbf{1}[v<1/2]+(1-v)\cdot\mathbf{1}[v\geq 1/2].

The claim now follows since 𝖤𝖢𝖤⁡(p,𝒟g)≤τ\mathsf{ECE}(p,\mathcal{D}^{g})\leq\tau. ∎

Often, the assumption of bounded 𝖤𝖢𝖤\mathsf{ECE} can be replaced with the weaker assumption that 𝐄[v​(p)​(y−p)]\E[v(p)(y-p)] is bounded for specific functions vv. Corollary 5.12.

Assume that pp is τ\tau-calibrated for 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g}. Then

𝖽𝗇𝗌𝒟𝒳​(μ𝖳𝖳𝖵)≥𝐄𝒟𝒳[2​p​(𝐱)​(1−p⁡(𝐱))]−2​τ.\mathsf{dns}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}(\mu_{\mathsf{TTV}})\geq\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[2p(\mathbf{x})(1-p(\mathbf{x}))]-2\tau.

so by Lemma 5.11 we have 𝐄𝒟𝒳[2​p​(𝐱)​(1−p⁡(𝐱))]∈[δ,2​δ]\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[2p(\mathbf{x})(1-p(\mathbf{x}))]\in[\delta,2\delta].

5.3 Hardcore Measures with Optimal Density

We now put together the ingredients to prove the existence of hardcore sets with optimal density.

Theorem 5.13.

For ε,δ,τ>0\varepsilon,\delta,\tau>0 where τ≤δ/2\tau\leq\delta/2, assume that pp is (w𝖬𝖺𝗑,𝒞,ε​δ)(w_{\mathsf{Max}},\mathcal{C},\varepsilon\delta)-multiaccurate for 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g}, and it is τ/4\tau/4-calibrated. Then the measure μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} is 2​δ−τ2\delta-\tau dense in 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, and gg is (1/2−ε)(1/2-\varepsilon)-hard for 𝒞\mathcal{C} under the distribution μ¯𝖬𝖺𝗑\bar{\mu}_{\mathsf{Max}}.

Proof.

By Lemma 5.10 applied with w𝖬𝖺𝗑w_{\mathsf{Max}}, we have

𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ𝖬𝖺𝗑)\displaystyle\mathsf{dns}(\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}) ≥2​𝐄𝒟𝒳[p​(𝐱)​(1−p​(𝐱))max⁡(p⁡(𝐱),1−p⁡(𝐱))]−τ/2\displaystyle\geq 2\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}\left[\frac{p(\mathbf{x})(1-p(\mathbf{x}))}{\max(p(\mathbf{x}),1-p(\mathbf{x}))}\right]-\tau/2
=2​𝐄𝒟𝒳[min⁡(p⁡(𝐱),1−p⁡(𝐱))]−τ/2\displaystyle=2\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\min(p(\mathbf{x}),1-p(\mathbf{x}))]-\tau/2
≥2​δ−τ/2−τ/2\displaystyle\geq 2\delta-\tau/2-\tau/2
≥2​δ−τ.\displaystyle\geq 2\delta-\tau.

where we use Lemma 5.11.

We can lower bound how hard gg is for 𝒞\mathcal{C} using Lemma 5.6 by

12−3​ε​δ2​(2​δ−τ)≥12−ε\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3\varepsilon\delta}{2(2\delta-\tau)}\geq\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon

for τ<0.5​δ\tau<0.5\delta. ∎

Next we consider the algorithmic complexity of obtaining a predictor that satisfies both calibration and (w𝖬𝖺𝗑,𝒞)(w_{\mathsf{Max}},\mathcal{C})-weighted multiaccuracy, assuming an oracle for (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) weak agnostic learning for 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Following previous work, we will consider the number of invocations to the weak agnostic learner. The key point is that since the only care about a single weight function w𝖬𝖺𝗑w_{\mathsf{Max}} which is bounded by 22, the complexity of the weighted versions of multiaccuracy and calibrated multiaccuracy are the same as their unweighted counterparts. The work of [17] which introduced calibrated multiaccuracy shows that its complexity is comparable to that of multiaccuracy, and much lower than multicalibration [17, Section 7]. This relies on ideas that are by now standard in the multicalibration literature [24, 19, 17], so we will provide a sketch.

Consider the problem of learning a predictor with (w𝖬𝖺𝗑,𝒞,α)(w_{\mathsf{Max}},\mathcal{C},\alpha) multiaccuracy, given access to an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C}. This can be done using the weighted multicalibration algorithm in [19, Section 5]. The main difference is that we have a single weight function w𝖬𝖺𝗑w_{\mathsf{Max}} rather than a set of weights, we consider binary rather than ll-class classification, and their analysis assumes a weak learner where β=α/2\beta=\alpha/2. We sketch the analysis below. Assume there exists c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} so that

𝐄[c⁡(𝐱)​w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p⁡(𝐱))​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))]≥α.\E[c(\mathbf{x})w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p(\mathbf{x}))(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))]\geq\alpha.

If we let 𝐳=w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p⁡(𝐱))​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))\mathbf{z}=w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p(\mathbf{x}))(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x})), then since 𝐲∈{0,1}\mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\} and p⁡(𝐱)∈[0,1]p(\mathbf{x})\in[0,1], |y−p⁡(𝐱)|≤max⁡{p⁡(𝐱),1−p⁡(𝐱)}|y-p(\mathbf{x})|\leq\max\{p(\mathbf{x}),1-p(\mathbf{x})\} and so 𝐳∈[−1,1]\mathbf{z}\in[-1,1], and we know 𝐄[c⁡(𝐱)​𝐳]≥α\E[c(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{z}]\geq\alpha. Hence by running our weak learner, we get hh such that 𝐄[h⁡(𝐱)​𝐳]≥β\E[h(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{z}]\geq\beta. Updating to p′​(𝐱)=p⁡(𝐱)+κ​β​w​(p⁡(𝐱))​h​(𝐱)p^{\prime}(\mathbf{x})=p(\mathbf{x})+\kappa\beta w(p(\mathbf{x}))h(\mathbf{x}) for a suitable constant κ\kappa reduces the squared loss by Ω⁡(β2)\Omega(\beta^{2}). This implies we will converge in O⁡(1/β2)O(1/\beta^{2}) iterations to a (w𝖬𝖺𝗑,𝒞,α)(w_{\mathsf{Max}},\mathcal{C},\alpha)-multiaccurate predictor. Essentially the same analysis works for all w∈Ww\in W, and the case when w=1w=1 is standard multiaccuracy.

To achieve calibration in addition to weighted multiaccuracy, we use the analysis of the calibrated multiaccuracy algorithm from [17, Section 7]. The key observation there is that if the calibration error is large, then recalibrating the predictor reduces the squared loss. Hence we can interleave recalibration steps with the calls to the weak learner, all the while ensuring that the squared loss decreases, and the number of calls to weak learner stays bounded by O⁡(1/β2)O(1/\beta^{2}).

Lastly, we use Theorem 5.13 to derive IHCL with optimal hardcore density 2​δ2\delta. We use the calibrated multiaccuracy algorithm from [17, Section 7] to bound the complexity 𝒞t,q\mathcal{C}_{t,q} of the class on which the input function gg is assumed to be δ\delta-hard.

Theorem 5.14.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a family of functions c:𝒳→{0,1}c:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\}, let 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} be a probability distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and let ϵ,δ,τ>0\epsilon,\delta,\tau>0. There exist t=O⁡((1/(ϵ2​δ2)+1/τ)⋅log⁡(|𝒳|/ϵ))t=O((1/(\epsilon^{2}\delta^{2})+1/\tau)\cdot\log(|\mathcal{X}|/\epsilon)), q=O⁡(1/(ϵ2​δ2))q=O(1/(\epsilon^{2}\delta^{2})) such that the following holds: If g:𝒳→{0,1}g:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\} is (𝒞t,q,δ)(\mathcal{C}_{t,q},\delta)-hard on 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, then there is a measure μ\mu satisfying:

  • •

    Hardness: gg is (𝒞,1/2−ϵ)(\mathcal{C},1/2-\epsilon)-hard on μ¯\bar{\mu}.

  • •

    Optimal density: 𝖽𝗇𝗌⁡(μ)=2​δ−τ\mathsf{dns}(\mu)=2\delta-\tau.

Proof.

We call the 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖬𝖠\mathsf{calMA} algorithm from [17] with 𝒞,𝒟g\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}^{g}, weight function w𝖬𝖺𝗑w_{\mathsf{Max}}, desired multiaccuracy error ϵ​δ\epsilon\delta, and desired calibrated error τ/4\tau/4, and obtain a (w𝖬𝖺𝗑,𝒞,ϵ​δ)(w_{\mathsf{Max}},\mathcal{C},\epsilon\delta)-multiaccurate and (τ/4)(\tau/4)-calibrated predictor pp for 𝒟g\mathcal{D}^{g}. Using this predictor pp, the input function gg, and the weight function w𝖬𝖺𝗑w_{\mathsf{Max}}, we construct the measure μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} as per Definition 5.4; namely, μ𝖬𝖺𝗑​(x)=w𝖬𝖺𝗑​(p⁡(x))⋅|g⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}(x)=w_{\mathsf{Max}}(p(x))\cdot|g(x)-p(x)|. By Theorem 5.13, this measure μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}} achieves the claimed hardness and optimal density stated in Theorem 5.14. For the 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖬𝖠\mathsf{calMA} algorithm, we assume access to a proper (ϵ​δ,ϵ​δ)(\epsilon\delta,\epsilon\delta)-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} under 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}; this satisfy the parameter requirements in [17, Alg. 2].1212 12 In [17], the total number of calls to an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner is analyzed. Here we are not concerned with the efficiency of the learner so we can assume a strong learner giving α=β\alpha=\beta.

By Theorem 7.7 in [17], the total number of calls to the learner during the execution of the 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖬𝖠\mathsf{calMA} algorithm is bounded by O⁡(1/(ϵ​δ)2)O(1/(\epsilon\delta)^{2}), which yields the claimed qq parameter. We remark that in their algorithm, the recalibration step does not call the weak agnostic learner, which is why the calibration error τ/4\tau/4 is not part of the qq parameter. As for the total number of gates in the circuit (i.e., the tt parameter), each iteration of the multiaccuracy step in the 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖬𝖠\mathsf{calMA} algorithm requires a scalar multiplication, a finite-precision addition, and a projection onto the interval [0,1][0,1]. As argued in [8, Appx. A], this can be handled by O⁡(log⁡(1/ϵ)+log⁡(1/|𝒳|)CLOSEO(\log(1/\epsilon)+\log(1/|\mathcal{X}|) gates, where we perform computations up to a fixed precision of Θ⁡(ϵ)\Theta(\epsilon) and log⁡(1/|𝒳|)\log(1/|\mathcal{X}|) corresponds to the bit-length of the elements in 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Lastly, the calibration-based steps in the 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖬𝖠\mathsf{calMA} algorithm do not require further calls to the learner, but they require computing all of the values of the predictor pp ([17, Lemma 7.4]). We discretize pp with parameter τ\tau, so that the interval [0,1][0,1] is partitioned into O⁡(1/τ)O(1/\tau) intervals. To compute the O⁡(1/τ)O(1/\tau) values of the predictor pp, we can use a lookup table of size O⁡(1/τ)O(1/\tau); such a lookup function can be computed by a circuit of size O⁡(1/τ)O(1/\tau) [2, §4]. ∎

The number of oracle gates in [8] and other optimal hardcore set constructions.

[8] uses the multicalibration algorithm to obtain a stronger and more general version of Impagliazzo’s hardcore lemma, IHCL+⁣+++. From it, they recover the IHCL theorem with density 2​δ2\delta. However, because this recovery is done through the multicalibration algorithm, the (t,q)(t,q) parameters for the class 𝒞t,q\mathcal{C}_{t,q}, although polynomial in 1/ϵ,1/δ1/\epsilon,1/\delta, are much larger than the ones we have obtained in Theorem 5.14. In particular, using the multicalibration algorithm presented in [18], we require q=O⁡(1/(ϵ6​δ6))q=O(1/(\epsilon^{6}\delta^{6})) calls to the weak agnostic learner [17]. When we recover the IHCL theorem from IHCL+⁣+++, the parameters further increase to q=1/(ϵ2​δ)6q=1/(\epsilon^{2}\delta)^{6} oracle gates.1313 13 This is because we can only glue together the pieces in the partition that are large enough and balanced enough; see [8, §3.3] for details.

Moreover, the dependence on ϵ\epsilon in the number of oracle calls qq that we make to the weak agnostic learner in our Theorem 5.14 is optimal. All boosting-based proofs of the hardcore lemma, starting with one of Impagliazzo’s original proofs and later generalized by Kilvans and Servedio to modularly use various boosting algorithms to obtain hardcore measures, need to call a weak learner O⁡(1/ϵ2)O(1/\epsilon^{2}) many times as to obtain constant density measure on which gg is (𝒞,1/2−ϵ)(\mathcal{C},1/2-\epsilon)-hard [35].

In particular, Impagliazzo’s boosting-based proof requires q=O⁡(1/(ϵ2​δ2))q=O(1/(\epsilon^{2}\delta^{2})) oracle calls [28, Thm. 1], and all subsequent hardcore constructions retain the dependence on 1/ϵ21/\epsilon^{2} in qq [35, 25], including the uniform versions of the hardcore lemma [47, 1, 49].

The size loss of O⁡(1/ϵ2)O(1/\epsilon^{2}) between the class 𝒞t,q\mathcal{C}_{t,q} (on which we assume the input function gg is mildly hard) and the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} (on which gg is strongly hard) is inevitable in all boosting-based proofs of IHCL [38], Blanc, Hayderi, Koch, and Tan recently showed that this circuit size loss is necessary and that these parameters are in fact optimal and inherent to the hardcore lemma, regardless of proof strategy [4]. The dependence on δ\delta can be improved: Nisan’s min-max proof in Impagliazzo’s original paper yields q=O⁡(1/ϵ2​log⁡(1/(ϵ​δ))CLOSEq=O(1/\epsilon^{2}\log(1/(\epsilon\delta)) [28, Lemma 2], and it was further improved to q=O⁡(1/ϵ2​log⁡(1/δ))q=O(1/\epsilon^{2}\log(1/\delta)) by Kilvans and Servedio who showed an elegant connection to boosting [35, Thm. 25]. But these proofs do not give the optimal density.

Deriving IHCL from IHCL+⁣+++.

The IHCL+⁣+++ theorem of [8] partitions the space 𝒳\mathcal{X} into level sets SvS_{v}. Within each level set, they construct a hardcore ℋv\mathcal{H}_{v} distribution of density 2​min⁡(v,1−v)2\min(v,1-v). We also know that 𝐄[min⁡(v,1−v)]≥δ\E[\min(v,1-v)]\geq\delta. To derive the IHCL with density 2​δ2\delta, we need to glue these distributions together to get a measure of density 2​δ2\delta. In their paper, [8] suggest the following gluing: sample SvS_{v} according to 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} and then sample within SvS_{v} from ℋv\mathcal{H}_{v}. This gluing as stated might not give a distribution with bounded density. The reason being that when we take convex combinations of distributions over disjoint regions, the min-entropy of the combination is the maximum of the min-entropies, not the average. A simple fix is to go from hardcore distributions to sets, and then take the union of sets.

We describe a different fix, which again leads to the measure μ𝖬𝖺𝗑\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}. From among all the measures that correspond to the distribution PvP_{v}, we pick the densest one, which happens to be |y−v|/max⁡(v,1−v)=μ𝖬𝖺𝗑​(v)|y-v|/\max(v,1-v)=\mu_{\mathsf{Max}}(v). This gives density 2​min⁡(v,1−v)2\min(v,1-v) on SvS_{v}. Intuitively, this gluing takes into account the value of vv (specifically, its closeness to 1/21/2) into account, so that we give more weight to the level sets SvS_{v} where gg is hardest to predict. Gluing densities is simple, since we define the functions independently on each SvS_{v}. The overall density is indeed the average of the densities on each piece, so it is 2​δ2\delta.

6 Restricted Weak Agnostic Learning and Multiacccuracy

Theorem 4.4 proves a reduction to multiaccuracy from (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learning for α>1/2\alpha>1/2. This motivates the study of weak learning in the setting where α\alpha is bounded away from 00. In this section, we investigate the notion of restricted weak agnostic learning, i.e., (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learning when α\alpha is bounded away from 00, and study what learning and fairness primitives can be derived from such restricted weak agnostic learners.

We begin by the observation that given any (restricted) (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C}, can we efficiently construct a (𝒞,α+εCLOSE(\mathcal{C},\alpha+\varepsilon)-multiaccurate predictor by the original multiaccuracy algorithm [24]. The following result is essentially proved in their paper and follows from the observation that if there is a multiaccuracy violation, then the weak agnostic learner can be used to provide a gradient update that reduces the potential function.

Theorem 6.1 ([24]).

For any concept class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} and parameters α,β\alpha,\beta, given access to a (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞\mathcal{C} for distributions with marginal 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}, one can produce a (𝒞,α+ε)(\mathcal{C},\alpha+\varepsilon)-multiaccurate predictor for 𝒟\mathcal{D} using O⁡(1/β2)O(1/\beta^{2}) oracle calls to the weak learner.

The remainder of the section is devoted to proving Theorem 6.5 below, which shows that (a) in general, (α′,β)(\alpha^{\prime},\beta)-weak agnostic learning cannot be reduced to (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-agnostic learning for α>α′\alpha>\alpha^{\prime}, (b) in general, we cannot obtain a predictor that is (𝒞,α/2−ε)(\mathcal{C},\alpha/2-\varepsilon)-multiaccurate given access to an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner. The latter result has a gap of a factor of two when viewed in conjunction with Theorem 6.1. While closing this is an interesting question, we observe that this is not possible for all values of α\alpha, e.g. when α=1\alpha=1, i.e., we only have realizable weak learning, it is still always possible to achieve (𝒞,1/2)(\mathcal{C},1/2)-multiaccuracy, by using the constant predictor p⁡(𝐱)=1/2p(\mathbf{x})=1/2.

Note that the task of (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) weak learning gets harder as

  • •

    α\alpha decreases, since this corresponds to detecting lower correlation.

  • •

    β\beta increases, since this corresponds to learning a better hypothesis.

The agnostic boosting results of [13, 30] tell us that increasing β\beta does not necessarily result in harder learning problems. They show that an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) weak learner implies a (γ,γ−α)(\gamma,\gamma-\alpha) weak learner for all γ>α\gamma>\alpha. This result is typically interpreted to say that if weak agnostic learning is possible for α\alpha approaching 00, then strong agnostic learning is possible.

It is natural to ask if there might be a similar boosting statement for α\alpha: that having an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) weak learner might imply an (α′,β′)(\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime}) weak learner for some values of α′<α\alpha^{\prime}<\alpha. We will show that such a result is unlikely, assuming the existence of standard cryptographic primitives.

For any α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and ε>0\varepsilon>0, we will show that there exist classes that are agnostically learnable in polynomial time given correlation α+ε\alpha+\varepsilon with the labels, but are hard to learn in polynomial time if the correlation is bounded by α\alpha. Further, in the former case, the learner only requires random samples and is a proper learner, but for the latter case, the weak learner is allowed query access, and is allowed to be improper. This result shows that weak learning indeed becomes easier as α\alpha increases, supporting our claim that multiaccuracy might be weaker as a learning primitive than weak agnostic learning.

Our construction of classes that are hard to learn assumes the existence of pseudorandom families of functions, and on the construction of binary error-correcting codes that can be (list)decoded from error rates approaching 1/21/2 [22]. Decoding from error rate 1/21/2 is information-theoretically impossible, since a random string would be at distance 1/21/2 from a codeword. The gap between distance 1/21/2 and 1/2−ε1/2-\varepsilon can be viewed as a gap of 00 versus 2​ε2\varepsilon in the correlation between the received word and codeword. Our result uses pseudorandom functions to translate this to a computational gap in the learnability of a suitably defined concept class with correlation α\alpha versus α+ε\alpha+\varepsilon. Our construction is inspired by a construction of Feldman [12] which he uses to show that membership queries add power to agnostic learning.

Assumption 6.2.

There exists a family of pseudorandom functions, denoted ℱ={fr:{0,1}n→{0,1}|r∈{0,1}n}\mathcal{F}=\{f_{r}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}~|~{r\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\}, such that

  • •

    frf_{r} can be computed in time poly⁡(n)\poly(n) given rr as input.

  • •

    For r←{0,1}nr\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{n} chosen uniformly at random, any (potentially randomized) algorithm that runs in time T⁡(n)T(n) and has query access to fr:{0,1}n→{0,1}f_{r}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} cannot distinguish it from a truly random function with advantage greater than 1/T⁡(n)1/T(n) over the uniform distribution on x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

Such functions are implied by the existence of one-way functions [15]. The time bound T⁡(n)T(n) of the distinguishers depend on the hardness of the one-way function. The most standard assumptions would imply there are no distinguishers with T⁡(n)=ncT(n)=n^{c}, for any constant cc. Often though, stronger assumptions are used where T⁡(n)T(n) is super-polynomial or even exponential.

The other key ingredient in our construction is binary error-correcting codes that can be list-decoded from high error rates in the worst case error model.

Definition 6.3.

A code Ecc:{0,1}n→{0,1}m\mathrm{Ecc}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{m} is said to be efficiently list decodable at radius δ\delta if given a received word w∈{0,1}mw\in\{0,1\}^{m} such that there exists x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} satisfying d⁡(w,Ecc⁡(x))≤δ​md(w,\mathrm{Ecc}(x))\leq\delta m, there is an algorithm that runs in time poly⁡(n)\poly(n) and returns a list containing xx with probability at least 0.90.9.

We will use constructions of binary error correcting codes that are efficiently list-decodable from error rate 1/2−ε1/2-\varepsilon. Such codes were first shown to exist by [22]. We will use their list-decoder for Reed-Solomon concatenated with Hadamard codes.

Lemma 6.4.

[22, Corollary 2] Let ε>0\varepsilon>0. For infinitely many nn, there exists a code RSH:{0,1}n→{0,1}m\mathrm{RSH}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{m} where m=O⁡(n2/ε4)m=O(n^{2}/\varepsilon^{4}) which is list-decodable at radius 1/2−ε1/2-\varepsilon in time poly⁡(n,1/ε)\poly(n,1/\varepsilon).1515 15 We ignore the question of what precise values of (n,m)(n,m) the code is defined for, but the underlying Reed-Solomon concatenated with Hadamard code family is defined for a fairly dense set of values.

While there have been subsequent improvements, our results only need m=poly⁡(n,1/ε)m=\poly(n,1/\varepsilon), which this construction guarantees.

Theorem 6.5.

For every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), there exists an instance space 𝒳=∪n𝒳n\mathcal{X}=\cup_{n}\mathcal{X}_{n}, distributions (𝒟𝒳n)n≥1(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}_{n}})_{n\geq 1} where D𝒳nD_{\mathcal{X}_{n}} is a distribution over 𝒳n\mathcal{X}_{n}, and a concept class 𝒞=∪n𝒞n\mathcal{C}=\cup_{n}\mathcal{C}_{n}, with 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} containing concepts over 𝒳n\mathcal{X}_{n}, such that:

  1. (i)

    There exists a learning algorithm LL, such that for every 0<ε<1−α0<\varepsilon<1-\alpha, n≥1n\geq 1, 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} is (α+ε,α)(\alpha+\varepsilon,\alpha)-weak agnostically learnable by LL in time poly⁡(n,1/ε)\poly(n,1/\varepsilon) for any distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} with marginal 𝒟𝒳n\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}_{n}}. The learner is proper and only requires only random examples.

  2. (ii)

    Under Assumption 6.2, there does not exist any learning algorithm LL that runs in time T⁡(n)/poly⁡(n)T(n)/\poly(n) that is an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner for 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} for any β≥2​α/T⁡(n)\beta\geq 2\alpha/T(n) for distributions with marginal 𝒟𝒳n\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}_{n}} over 𝒳n\mathcal{X}_{n}, and succeeds with probability at least 1/T⁡(n)1/T(n), even with access to membership queries.

  3. (iii)

    Under Assumption 6.2, for any 0<ε<min⁡{α,1−α}0<\varepsilon<\min\{\alpha,1-\alpha\}, there does not exist any algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that runs in time T⁡(n)/poly⁡(n,1/ε)T(n)/\poly(n,1/\varepsilon) and outputs with probability at least 1/T⁡(n)1/T(n), a predictor p:𝒳n→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}_{n}\rightarrow[0,1] that is (𝒞n,α/2−ϵ)(\mathcal{C}_{n},\alpha/2-\epsilon)-multiaccurate for distributions with marginal 𝒟𝒳n\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}_{n}} over 𝒳n\mathcal{X}_{n}, even with access to membership queries.

Proof.

The basic setup for the three parts of the theorem are the same which we first describe. For simplicity we will drop the subscript nn, keeping the dependence on nn implicit. Let mm be as in Lemma 6.4, and let E=[m]E=[m] and F={0,1}nF=\{0,1\}^{n}. We take 𝒳=E∪F\mathcal{X}=E\cup F, equipped with the marginal distribution 𝒟𝒳\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} so that Pr𝒟𝒳[𝐱∈E]=1−α\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mathbf{x}\in E]=1-\alpha and Pr𝒟𝒳[𝐱∈F]=α\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\mathbf{x}\in F]=\alpha and the conditional distribution on each of EE and FF is uniform. We will index the coordinates of RSH\mathrm{RSH} using EE and denote the 𝐱th\mathbf{x}^{\textit{th}} coordinate of the encoding of rr by RSH\mathrm{RSH} as RSH​(r)𝐱\mathrm{RSH}(r)_{\mathbf{x}} for each 𝐱∈E\mathbf{x}\in E.

For each random seed r∈{0,1}nr\in\{0,1\}^{n}, we define a Boolean function gr:𝒳→{0,1}g_{r}:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} so that on the set EE, grg_{r} is the encoding of rr using RSH\mathrm{RSH} whereas on FF, grg_{r} equals the pseudorandom function frf_{r}. Formally:

gr​(𝐱)={RSH​(r)𝐱​for​𝐱∈Efr​(𝐱)​for​𝐱∈F\displaystyle g_{r}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}\mathrm{RSH}(r)_{\mathbf{x}}\ \text{for}\ \mathbf{x}\in E\\ f_{r}(\mathbf{x})\ \text{for}\ \mathbf{x}\in F\end{cases}

We then define the {±1}\{\pm 1\} version of grg_{r} as cr​(𝐱)=2​gr​(𝐱)−1c_{r}(\mathbf{x})=2g_{r}(\mathbf{x})-1 and let 𝒞={cr|r∈{0,1}n}\mathcal{C}=\{c_{r}~|~{r\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\}.

Part (i): For the positive result in Part (i), consider any distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} on (𝐱,𝐲)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) where 𝐱∼𝒟𝒳\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}} and there exists cr∈𝒞c_{r}\in\mathcal{C} such that cor⁡(𝐲,cr​(𝐱))≥α+ε\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r}(\mathbf{x}))\geq\alpha+\varepsilon. It must hold that cor⁡(𝐲,cr​(𝐱)|𝐱∈E)≥ε/(1−α)\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r}(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\in E)\geq\varepsilon/(1-\alpha), since if this were not true, we reach a contradiction as

cor⁡(𝐲,cr)\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r}) =(1−α)⋅cor⁡(𝐲,cr|𝐱∈E)+α⋅cor⁡(𝐲,cr|𝐱∈F)\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)\cdot\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r}|\mathbf{x}\in E)+\alpha\cdot\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r}|\mathbf{x}\in F)
<(1−α)​ε1−α+α\displaystyle<(1-\alpha)\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\alpha}+\alpha
=α+ε.\displaystyle=\alpha+\varepsilon.

Using the standard translation from correlation to Hamming distance for variables in {±1}\{\pm 1\},

cor⁡(𝐲,cr​(𝐱)|𝐱∈E)\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r}(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\in E) =𝐄[cr​(𝐱)​(2​𝐲−1)|𝐱∈E]\displaystyle=\E[c_{r}(\mathbf{x})(2\mathbf{y}-1)|\mathbf{x}\in E]
=𝐄[(2​gr​(𝐱)−1)​(2​𝐲−1)|𝐱∈E]\displaystyle=\E[(2g_{r}(\mathbf{x})-1)(2\mathbf{y}-1)|\mathbf{x}\in E]
=1−2​Pr⁡[𝐲≠gr​(𝐱)|𝐱∈E].\displaystyle=1-2\Pr[\mathbf{y}\neq g_{r}(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\in E].

Since the LHS is at least ε/(1−α)\varepsilon/(1-\alpha), and gr​(x)g_{r}(x) equals RSH​(r)x\mathrm{RSH}(r)_{x} on the set EE, we conclude that

Pr(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟⁡[𝐲≠RSH​(r)𝐱|𝐱∈E]≤12​(1−ε1−α)≤(1−ε−ε​α)2\displaystyle\Pr_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathbf{y}\neq\mathrm{RSH}(r)_{\mathbf{x}}|\mathbf{x}\in E]\leq\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\alpha}\right)\leq\frac{(1-\varepsilon-\varepsilon\alpha)}{2}

We wait until we see a sample (𝐱=x,𝐲)(\mathbf{x}=x,\mathbf{y}) for every x∈[m]x\in[m], which takes O⁡(m​log⁡(m)/(1−α))O(m\log(m)/(1-\alpha)) samples, form a received word 𝐰\mathbf{w} and decode it using the list-decoding algorithm. We can write

𝐄[d⁡(𝐰,RSH⁡(r))]\displaystyle\E[d(\mathbf{w},\mathrm{RSH}(r))] =𝐄[∑x∈[m]𝟏[𝐰(x)≠RSH(r)x]]\displaystyle=\E\left[\sum_{x\in[m]}\mathbf{1}[\mathbf{w}(x)\neq\mathrm{RSH}(r)_{x}]\right]
=∑x∈[m]Pr[𝐰(x)≠RSH(r)x]\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in[m]}\Pr[\mathbf{w}(x)\neq\mathrm{RSH}(r)_{x}]
=∑x∈[m]Pr⁡[𝐲≠RSH​(r)x|𝐱=x]\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in[m]}\Pr[\mathbf{y}\neq\mathrm{RSH}(r)_{x}|\mathbf{x}=x]
=m​Pr(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟​[𝐲≠RSH​(r)𝐱|𝐱∈E]\displaystyle=m\Pr_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathbf{y}\neq\mathrm{RSH}(r)_{\mathbf{x}}|\mathbf{x}\in E]
≤(1−ε−ε​α)2​m.\displaystyle\leq\frac{(1-\varepsilon-\varepsilon\alpha)}{2}m.

Hence by a Chernoff bound, with probability 1−exp⁡(−ε2​α2​m)1-\exp(-\varepsilon^{2}\alpha^{2}m) we have d⁡(𝐰,RSH⁡(r))≤(1−ε)​m/2d(\mathbf{w},\mathrm{RSH}(r))\leq(1-\varepsilon)m/2. So running the list-decoder from random samples returns a list containing the seed rr. We can enumerate over all candidates r′r^{\prime} in the list, and check whether cor⁡(𝐲,cr′)≥α\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r^{\prime}})\geq\alpha using random samples, using the fact that frf_{r} is easy to compute given rr. Taking r′=rr^{\prime}=r will give α+ε\alpha+\varepsilon correlation, but there might be better hypotheses. We output the best hypothesis that we find, which will have correlation at least α\alpha with probability 0.90.9.1616 16 We lose an ε\varepsilon in accounting for sampling error in estimating the true correlation. We can amplify the probability of success through repetition.

Part (ii): For the negative result in Part (ii), we define a distribution 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r} where we draw r∈{0,1}nr\in\{0,1\}^{n} at random. Then 𝐲|𝐱\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x} is a uniformly random bit for 𝐱∈E\mathbf{x}\in E and 𝐲|𝐱=fr​(𝐱)\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}=f_{r}(\mathbf{x}) for 𝐱∈F\mathbf{x}\in F. In essence, 𝐲|𝐱\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x} is a truly random function on EE and a pseudorandom function on FF. If we take the hypothesis crc_{r}, then it achieves no correlation on EE, and perfect correlation on FF, so that cor⁡(𝐲,cr)=α\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r})=\alpha.

On the other hand, consider an efficient learning algorithm which runs in time T⁡(n)T(n), is allowed query access to 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and outputs a hypothesis h:𝒳→[−1,1]h:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1] that achieves correlation β\beta. Then,

β\displaystyle\beta =(1−α)⋅cor⁡(𝐲,h⁡(𝐱)|𝐱∈E)+α⋅cor⁡(𝐲,h⁡(𝐱)|𝐱∈F)\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)\cdot\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},h(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\in E)+\alpha\cdot\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},h(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\in F)
=α⋅cor⁡(fr​(𝐱),h⁡(𝐱)|𝐱∈F).\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\mathrm{cor}(f_{r}(\mathbf{x}),h(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\in F).

But this implies that cor⁡(fr​(𝐱),h⁡(𝐱)|𝐱∈F)≥β/α\mathrm{cor}(f_{r}(\mathbf{x}),h(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\in F)\geq\beta/\alpha, so hh (restricted to FF) has distinguishing advantage β/(2​α)\beta/(2\alpha) for frf_{r} versus a random function, which is a contradiction if β≥2​α/T⁡(n)\beta\geq 2\alpha/T(n).

Part (iii): Finally, for the negative result in Part (iii), consider the same distribution 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r} defined in Part (ii) above. As observed above cor⁡(𝐲,cr)=α\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r})=\alpha. Suppose pp is a (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate predictor for 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r} for τ≤α/2−ε\tau\leq\alpha/2-\varepsilon. Let 𝐲p\mathbf{y}_{p} denote the Bernoulli random variable corresponding to p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}), i.e., 𝐄[𝐲p|p⁡(𝐱)]=p⁡(𝐱)\E[\mathbf{y}_{p}|p(\mathbf{x})]=p(\mathbf{x}). Then we observe that since pp is (OPEN𝒞,τ)\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate,

|cor⁡(𝐲,cr)−cor⁡(𝐲p,cr)|\displaystyle\left|\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r})-\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y}_{p},c_{r})\right| ≤|𝐄[cr​(𝐱)​(2​𝐲−1)−cr​(𝐱)​(2​𝐲p−1)]|\displaystyle\leq\left|\E[c_{r}(\mathbf{x})(2\mathbf{y}-1)-c_{r}(\mathbf{x})(2\mathbf{y}_{p}-1)]\right|
≤2​|𝐄[cr​(𝐱)​(𝐲−𝐲p)]|\displaystyle\leq 2\left|\E[c_{r}(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{y}_{p})]\right|
≤2​|𝐄[cr​(𝐱)​(𝐲−p⁡(𝐱))]|\displaystyle\leq 2\left|\E[c_{r}(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-p(\mathbf{x}))]\right|
≤α−2​ε.\displaystyle\leq\alpha-2\varepsilon.

Since cor⁡(𝐲,cr)≥α\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},c_{r})\geq\alpha, this implies that cor⁡(𝐲p,cr)≥2​ε\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y}_{p},c_{r})\geq 2\varepsilon.

We will show that such a predictor pp can be used to predict frf_{r} with non-trivial probability, which contradicts Assumption 6.2. Since

cor⁡(𝐲p,cr)\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y}_{p},c_{r}) =(1−α)⋅cor⁡(𝐲p,cr|𝐱∈E)+α⋅cor⁡(𝐲p,cr|𝐱∈F),\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)\cdot\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y}_{p},c_{r}|\mathbf{x}\in E)+\alpha\cdot\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y}_{p},c_{r}|\mathbf{x}\in F),

either cor⁡(𝐲p,cr|𝐱∈E)≥ε/(1−α)\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y}_{p},c_{r}|\mathbf{x}\in E)\geq\varepsilon/(1-\alpha), or cor⁡(𝐲p,cr|𝐱∈F)≥ε/α\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y}_{p},c_{r}|\mathbf{x}\in F)\geq\varepsilon/\alpha. In the former case, we can use list decoding to obtain rr and thence frf_{r} as in Part (i). For the latter case, we observe that 𝐲p\mathbf{y}_{p} lets us predict frf_{r} with non-trivial advantage, since

𝐄𝐱∼uF[fr(𝐱)≠𝐲p]\displaystyle\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim_{u}F}\left[f_{r}(\mathbf{x})\neq\mathbf{y}_{p}\right] =12𝐄𝐱∼uF[1−(2𝐲p−1)(2fr(𝐱)−1)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim_{u}F}\left[1-(2\mathbf{y}_{p}-1)(2f_{r}(\mathbf{x})-1)\right]
=12−12𝐄𝐱∼uF[(2𝐲p−1)cr(𝐱)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim_{u}F}[(2\mathbf{y}_{p}-1)c_{r}(\mathbf{x})]
=12−12​cor​(𝐲p,cr|𝐱∈F)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y}_{p},c_{r}|\mathbf{x}\in F)

where we use cr​(x)=2​fr​(x)−1c_{r}(x)=2f_{r}(x)-1 for x∈Fx\in F. Thus, in either case we can predict the pseudorandom function frf_{r} with non-trivial advantage with non-negligible probability. This concludes the proof of the result. ∎

7 Conclusion and Future Work

We have shown in this paper that multiaccuracy, together with global calibration, is a fairly powerful notion that has implications for agnostic learning and (optimal) hardcore set constructions. However, our work leaves open several open questions.

An immediate one is closing the gap in Theorem 6.5 which only shows that an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner does not yield anything better than (𝒞,α/2)(\mathcal{C},\alpha/2)-multiaccuracy; however, Theorem 6.1 only shows that it is possible to achive (𝒞,α)(\mathcal{C},\alpha)-multiaccuracy using access to an (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-weak agnostic learner.

Another natural question is whether more general reductions to multiaccuracy can yield a weak agnostic learner. The result in Theorem 4.1 only rules out learners obtained by post-processing a predictor satisfying certain multigroup guarantees. A stronger model would be to consider an algorithm that has oracle access to a learner that for multiaccurate predictors, which it can call multiple times. In Appendix A, we show how a more general post-processing involving points x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} in addition to just the value p⁡(x)p(x) can in some cases yield agnostic learners.

Lastly, by the equivalence between the Regularity Lemma by [46] and the multiaccuracy theorem, multicalibration implies stronger and more general versions of other well-known theorems in complexity theory besides the hardcore lemma, such as the Dense Model Theorem and characterizations of pseudo-average min-entropy [44, 48, 8], and Yao’s XOR lemma [40]. Similar to our result for Impagliazzo’s Hardcore Lemma, it is natural to ask if versions of these theorems can be proved under weaker assumptions like calibrated multiaccuracy.

Appendix A Projecting Multiaccurate Predictors onto the Span of 𝒞\mathcal{C}

Intuitively, the reason why 𝒞\mathcal{C}-multiaccuracy does not directly imply weak agnostic learning for the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} is that multiaccuracy only implies a certain type of closeness between the predictor pp and the labels 𝐲\mathbf{y} over the span of the concept class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Let p∗p^{*} denote the Bayes optimal predictor, i.e., p∗​(𝐱)=𝐄[𝐲|𝐱]p^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\E[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}], and suppose for now that pp satisfies (𝒞,0)(\mathcal{C},0)-multiaccuracy for 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Let p~∗=2​p∗−1\tilde{p}^{*}=2p^{*}-1 and p~=2​p−1\tilde{p}=2p-1 denote the [−1,1][-1,1] versions of the predictors p∗p^{*} and pp. Let 𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}) denote the vector space spanned by 𝒞\mathcal{C}. We can write,

p~=p~C+p~⟂​ and ​p~∗=p~C∗+p~⟂∗,\tilde{p}=\tilde{p}_{C}+\tilde{p}_{\perp}\text{~~and~~}\tilde{p}^{*}=\tilde{p}^{*}_{C}+\tilde{p}^{*}_{\perp},

where p~C,p~C∗\tilde{p}_{C},\tilde{p}^{*}_{C} are the components of p~\tilde{p} and p~∗\tilde{p}^{*} in the 𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}) respectively, and p~⟂,p~⟂∗\tilde{p}_{\perp},\tilde{p}^{*}_{\perp} are the components of p~,p~∗\tilde{p},\tilde{p}^{*} orthogonal to 𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}). We recall that the inner product ⟨f,g⟩\langle f,g\rangle for functions f,g:𝒳→ℝf,g:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} is defined by 𝐄𝒟𝒳[f⁡(𝐱)​g​(𝐱)]\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[f(\mathbf{x})g(\mathbf{x})]. Since pp is (𝒞,0)(\mathcal{C},0)-multiaccurate for 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we have that,

⟨c,p~−p~∗⟩=2𝐄[c(𝐱)(p(𝐱)−p∗(𝐱))]=0\langle c,\tilde{p}-\tilde{p}^{*}\rangle=2\E[c(\mathbf{x})(p(\mathbf{x})-p^{*}(\mathbf{x}))]=0

for every c∈Cc\in C; i.e., p~−p~∗\tilde{p}-\tilde{p}^{*} is orthogonal to 𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}). But

p~−p~∗=p~C−p~C∗+p~⟂−p~⟂∗.\tilde{p}-\tilde{p}^{*}=\tilde{p}_{C}-\tilde{p}_{C}^{*}+\tilde{p}_{\perp}-\tilde{p}_{\perp}^{*}.

As p~⟂,p~⟂∗\tilde{p}_{\perp},\tilde{p}^{*}_{\perp} are both orthogonal to 𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}), and p~C−p~C∗∈𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\tilde{p}_{C}-\tilde{p}^{*}_{C}\in\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}), we must have p~C=p~C∗\tilde{p}_{C}=\tilde{p}^{*}_{C}. What this suggests is that even though technically we can have

cor⁡(𝐲,2​p−1)=⟨p~∗,p~⟩=𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[(2​p∗​(𝐱)−1)​(2​p​(x)−1)]=0\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},2p-1)=\langle\tilde{p}^{*},\tilde{p}\rangle=\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[(2p^{*}(\mathbf{x})-1)(2p(x)-1)]=0

as Theorem 4.1 indicates, we can conclude that,

cor⁡(𝐲,p~C)=⟨p~∗,p~C⟩\displaystyle\mathrm{cor}(\mathbf{y},\tilde{p}_{C})=\langle\tilde{p}^{*},\tilde{p}_{C}\rangle =⟨p~C∗+p~⟂∗,p~C⟩\displaystyle=\langle\tilde{p}^{*}_{C}+\tilde{p}^{*}_{\perp},\tilde{p}_{C}\rangle
=⟨p~C∗,p~C⟩+⟨p~⟂∗,p~C⟩\displaystyle=\langle\tilde{p}^{*}_{C},\tilde{p}_{C}\rangle+\langle\tilde{p}^{*}_{\perp},\tilde{p}_{C}\rangle
=‖p~C∗‖22.\displaystyle=\|\tilde{p}^{*}_{C}\|_{2}^{2}.

Above in the last line we used that p~⟂∗\tilde{p}^{*}_{\perp} is orthogonal to 𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}) and that p~C∈𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\tilde{p}_{C}\in\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}), as well as the observation that p~C=p~C∗\tilde{p}_{C}=\tilde{p}^{*}_{C}. Thus, a projection of p~\tilde{p} onto 𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}) could potentially lead to a weak agnostic learner. However, we need to take some care as (a) p~C\tilde{p}_{C} need not have range [−1,1][-1,1] (or be bounded even), and (b) if we don’t have (𝒞,0)(\mathcal{C},0)-multiaccuracy, but only (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau), then depending on the representation of p~C\tilde{p}_{C} in terms of c∈Cc\in C, the errors could accumulate making the above analysis trivial. Observe that this constitutes a much richer form of post-processing that considered in Section 4.

In this section, we make this intuition more precise.

Theorem A.1.

Let p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1] satisfy (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccuracy for 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Suppose we have q=∑sλ​csq=\sum_{s}\lambda c_{s} for cs∈𝒞c_{s}\in\mathcal{C}, satisfying,

𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[((2​p​(𝐱)−1)−q⁡(𝐱))2]≤𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[(2​p​(𝐱)−1)2]−γ.\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[((2p(\mathbf{x})-1)-q(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]\leq\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)^{2}]-\gamma.

Let h=clip⁡(q)h=\clip(q), which is clipped to have h⁡(𝐱)∈[−1,1]h(\mathbf{x})\in[-1,1] for all 𝐱∈𝒳\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}. Then,

𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[((2​𝐲−1)−h⁡(𝐱))2]≤1−γ+4​τ​∑s|λs|.\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[((2\mathbf{y}-1)-h(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]\leq 1-\gamma+4\tau\sum_{s}|\lambda_{s}|.
Proof.

For simplicity, let p~=2​p−1\tilde{p}=2p-1 denote the [−1,1][-1,1]-version of pp. Then,

γ\displaystyle\gamma ≤𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[p~​(𝐱)2]−𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[(p~​(𝐱)−q⁡(𝐱))2]\displaystyle\leq\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\tilde{p}(\mathbf{x})^{2}]-\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[(\tilde{p}(\mathbf{x})-q(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]
=2​𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[p~​(𝐱)​q​(𝐱)]−𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[q​(𝐱)2]\displaystyle=2\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[\tilde{p}(\mathbf{x})q(\mathbf{x})]-\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[q(\mathbf{x})^{2}]
=2​𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[(2​𝐲−1)​q​(𝐱)]−𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[q​(𝐱)2]+2​𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[q⁡(𝐱)​(p~​(𝐱)−(2​𝐲−1))]\displaystyle=2\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[(2\mathbf{y}-1)q(\mathbf{x})]-\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[q(\mathbf{x})^{2}]+2\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[q(\mathbf{x})(\tilde{p}(\mathbf{x})-(2\mathbf{y}-1))]
=2​𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[(2​𝐲−1)​q​(𝐱)]−𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[q​(𝐱)2]+4​𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[q⁡(𝐱)​(p⁡(𝐱)−y⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle=2\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[(2\mathbf{y}-1)q(\mathbf{x})]-\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[q(\mathbf{x})^{2}]+4\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[q(\mathbf{x})(p(\mathbf{x})-y(\mathbf{x}))]
=2​𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[(2​𝐲−1)​q​(𝐱)]−𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[q​(𝐱)2]+4​∑sλs​𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[cs​(𝐱)​(p⁡(𝐱)−𝐲)]\displaystyle=2\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[(2\mathbf{y}-1)q(\mathbf{x})]-\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[q(\mathbf{x})^{2}]+4\sum_{s}\lambda_{s}\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[c_{s}(\mathbf{x})(p(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{y})]
≤𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[(2​𝐲−1)2]−𝐄(𝐱,𝐲)∼𝒟[((2​𝐲−1)−q⁡(𝐱))2]+4​τ​∑s|λs|\displaystyle\leq\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[(2\mathbf{y}-1)^{2}]-\E_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[((2\mathbf{y}-1)-q(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]+4\tau\sum_{s}|\lambda_{s}|

Together, Theorem A.1 and Theorem 3.5 imply that a certain type of projection onto 𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗇⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{span}(\mathcal{C}), particularly one that is ℓ1\ell_{1}-sparse, suffices for weak agnostic learning:

Corollary A.2.

Let p:𝒳→[0,1]p:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1] satisfy (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccuracy for 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Suppose we have q=∑sλs​csq=\sum_{s}\lambda_{s}c_{s} for cs∈𝒞c_{s}\in\mathcal{C}, satisfying,

𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[((2​p​(𝐱)−1)−q⁡(𝐱))2]≤𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[(2​p​(𝐱)−1)2]−γ.\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[((2p(\mathbf{x})-1)-q(\mathbf{x}))^{2}]\leq\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)^{2}]-\gamma.

for γ≥4​τ​∑s|λs|+β\gamma\geq 4\tau\sum_{s}|\lambda_{s}|+\beta. Then, h=clip⁡(q)h=\clip(q), which clips qq to the range [−1,1][-1,1], satisfies cor𝒟​(𝐲,h)≥β\mathrm{cor}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{y},h)\geq\beta.

𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[((2​p​(𝐱)−1)−q⁡(𝐱))2]\displaystyle\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[((2p(\mathbf{x})-1)-q(\mathbf{x}))^{2}] =𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[(2​p​(𝐱)−1)2]−2​𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[(2​p​(𝐱)−1)​q​(𝐱)]+𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[q​(𝐱)2]\displaystyle=\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)^{2}]-2\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)q(\mathbf{x})]+\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[q(\mathbf{x})^{2}]

≤𝐄𝐱∼𝒟𝒳[(2​p​(𝐱)−1)2]−α2.\displaystyle\leq\E_{\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{X}}}[(2p(\mathbf{x})-1)^{2}]-\alpha^{2}.

In the last inequality, we used cor⁡(p,c)≥α\mathrm{cor}(p,c)\geq\alpha and ‖c‖≤1\|c\|\leq 1, as cc has range [−1,1][-1,1].

A.1 Multiaccuracy as a Query Oracle

A natural question is whether there are any cases where such ℓ1\ell_{1}-sparse projections are possible. One advantage of having access to the predictor pp rather than just examples (𝐱,𝐲)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) drawn from 𝒟\mathcal{D} is that we may query the predictor pp at any point 𝐱∈𝒳\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X} of our choice. As a result, if we have a proper learning algorithm for a class 𝒞\mathcal{C} that uses membership queries, then we can learn such a class only with random examples and access to a multiaccurate predictor pp.

Theorem A.3.

Suppose the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} (that contains the constant function 11) is efficiently properly agnostically learnable with access to random examples from 𝒟\mathcal{D} and query access to the target function to accuracy ε\varepsilon, then provided we have access to a (C,τ)(C,\tau)-multiaccurate predictor pp for 𝒟\mathcal{D}, 𝒞\mathcal{C} is efficiently properly agnostically learnable using only access to random examples from 𝒟\mathcal{D} and (using the predictor pp) to accuracy ε+3​τ\varepsilon+3\tau.

Proof.

In this proof, we will assume that the target function ff takes values in {0,1}\{0,1\} and also that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a class of functions from 𝒳→{0,1}\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the algorithm for efficiently agnostically learning 𝒞\mathcal{C} using the random examples from 𝒟\mathcal{D} and query access to the target function and pp be the (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate predictor for 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Since pp may not be Boolean, we denote by 𝐙p⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{Z}_{p(\mathbf{x})} a (freshly independently drawn each time) Bernoulli random variable with parameter p⁡(𝐱)p(\mathbf{x}). When the algorithm draws a random example, we replace (𝐱,𝐲)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}), by (𝐱,𝐙p⁡(𝐱))(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{Z}_{p(\mathbf{x})}) and we simulate queries by returning 𝐙p⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{Z}_{p(\mathbf{x})} when queried with point 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Then, we are guaranteed that 𝒜\mathcal{A} returns c𝒜∈𝒞c_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathcal{C}, such that with probability at least 0.990.99,

err⁡(c𝒜,𝒟)\displaystyle\mathrm{err}(c_{\mathcal{A}};\mathcal{D}) ≤minc∈𝒞⁡𝐄[|c⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱)|]+ε\displaystyle\leq\min_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\E[|c(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x})|]+\varepsilon

Let f:𝒳→{0,1}f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\{0,1\} denote the target, i.e. we get (𝐱,f⁡(𝐱))(\mathbf{x},f(\mathbf{x})) from 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Then, we have the following,

Pr[c(𝐱)≠f(𝐱)]\displaystyle\Pr[c(\mathbf{x})\neq f(\mathbf{x})] =𝐄[c⁡(𝐱)​(1−f⁡(𝐱))+(1−c⁡(𝐱))​f​(𝐱)]\displaystyle=\E[c(\mathbf{x})(1-f(\mathbf{x}))+(1-c(\mathbf{x}))f(\mathbf{x})]
=𝐄[c(𝐱)+f(𝐱)]−2𝐄[c(𝐱)f(𝐱)]\displaystyle=\E[c(\mathbf{x})+f(\mathbf{x})]-2\E[c(\mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x})]
≤𝐄[c(𝐱)+p(𝐱)]−2𝐄[c(𝐱)p(𝐱)]+3τ\displaystyle\leq\E[c(\mathbf{x})+p(\mathbf{x})]-2\E[c(\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})]+3\tau
=𝐄[c⁡(𝐱)​(1−p⁡(𝐱))+(1−c⁡(𝐱))​p​(𝐱)]+3​τ\displaystyle=\E[c(\mathbf{x})(1-p(\mathbf{x}))+(1-c(\mathbf{x}))p(\mathbf{x})]+3\tau
=𝐄[|c⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱)|]+3​τ.\displaystyle=\E[|c(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x})|]+3\tau.
Similarly, we may show that
Pr[c(𝐱)≠f(𝐱)]\displaystyle\Pr[c(\mathbf{x})\neq f(\mathbf{x})] ≥𝐄[|c⁡(𝐱)−p⁡(𝐱)|]−3​τ.\displaystyle\geq\E[|c(\mathbf{x})-p(\mathbf{x})|]-3\tau.

Above we have used that pp is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate for 𝒟\mathcal{D} as well as assumed that the constant 𝟏\mathbf{1} function is in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Thus, we get that,

err⁡(c𝒜,𝒟)\displaystyle\mathrm{err}(c_{\mathcal{A}};\mathcal{D}) ≤minc∈C⁡err⁡(c,𝒟)+ε+3​δ.\displaystyle\leq\min_{c\in C}\mathrm{err}(c;\mathcal{D})+\varepsilon+3\delta.

∎

When considering learning functions defined over {−1,1}n\{-1,1\}^{n} with respect to the uniform (or in some cases a product) distribution over the domain, a classical result of Goldreich and Levin shows that with query access to the target function, we can identify all the heavy Fourier coefficients. Essentially this algorithm allows us to find projections as required by Theorem A.1; this also gives a proper agnostic learning algorithm for the class of parities. We briefly the Goldreich-Levin algorithm below.

The Goldreich-Levin algorithm.

By the Fourier expansion theorem we know that every function f:{−1,1}→ℝf:\{-1,1\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} can be uniquely expressed as a multilinear polynomial:

f⁡(x)=∑S⊆[n]f^​(S)​χS,f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}(S)\chi_{S},

where χS​(x)=∏i∈Sxi\chi_{S}(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_{i} for x=(x1,…,xn)∈ℝnx=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and f^​(S)=𝐄x∼{−1,1}n[f⁡(x)​χS]\widehat{f}(S)=\E_{x\sim\{-1,1\}^{n}}[f(x)\chi_{S}] denotes the Fourier coefficient of ff on SS. Again defining the inner product ⟨f,g⟩\langle f,g\rangle between two functions f,g:{−1,1}n→ℝf,g:\{-1,1\}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} as 𝐄x∼{−1,1}n[f⁡(x)​g​(x)]\E_{x\sim\{-1,1\}^{n}}[f(x)g(x)] we see that the 2n2^{n} parity functions χS:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}\chi_{S}:\{-1,1\}^{n}\rightarrow\{-1,1\} form an orthonormal basis for the vector space of functions {−1,1}n→ℝ\{-1,1\}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} [42, Thm. 1.5]. The Goldreich-Levin algorithm finds the largest Fourier coefficients of a function given membership access to it:

Theorem A.4 (Goldreich-Levin [16]).

Given query access to f:{−1,1}n→[−1,1]f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1], and given γ,δ>0\gamma,\delta>0, there is a poly​(n,1γ,log⁡1δ)\text{poly}(n,\frac{1}{\gamma},\log\frac{1}{\delta})-time algorithm that outputs a list L={S1,…,Sm}L=\{S_{1},\dots,S_{m}\} such that:

  1. 1.

    If f^​(S)≥γ\widehat{f}(S)\geq\gamma, then S∈LS\in L, and

  2. 2.

    If S∈LS\in L, then f^​(S)≥γ2\widehat{f}(S)\geq\frac{\gamma}{2} holds with probability 1−δ1-\delta.

Using Theorem A.3, we can observe the following simple corollary which shows that finding pp that is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-accurate for 𝒟\mathcal{D}, where the marginal distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X} is uniform, is at least as hard as Learning Parities with Noise (LPN). Since LPN is widely believed to be hard, we can conclude that the existence of an efficient algorithm that produces a pp that is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate for small values of τ\tau is unlikely to exist, at least when the marginal distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X} is uniform.

Corollary A.5.

When 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the class of parities, and 𝒟\mathcal{D} is such that the marginal distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X} is uniform, then finding pp that is (𝒞,τ)(\mathcal{C},\tau)-multiaccurate for 𝒟\mathcal{D} and τ≤0.1\tau\leq 0.1 is at least as hard as properly agnostically learning 𝒞\mathcal{C} with random classification noise with noise rate 0.10.1.

Proof.

We know that the class of parities is efficiently properly agnostically learnable using the Goldreich-Levin or the Kushilevitz-Mansour algorithm [16, 37]. Since the noise rate is 0.10.1, we know that there the optimal error is at most 0.10.1, then using Theorem A.3 we can find a parity that has error at most 0.4+ε<1/20.4+\varepsilon<1/2. However, in the random classification noise setting all parities, except the target parity are uncorrelated with the target labels, so in fact we must have identified the target parity. ∎
